On the Grothendieck Ring of Finite-Dimensional Non-Degenerate Evolution AlgebrasThanks: This work was partially supported by MCIN/AEI/10.13039/501100011033 [PID2023-149804NB-I00 to C.C., and A.V].

Abstract.

We study the Grothendieck ring of finite-dimensional non-degenerate evolution algebras over a field 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}, with addition induced by direct sum and multiplication induced by tensor product. Although its underlying abelian group is freely generated by indecomposable isomorphism classes, the ring structure is much smaller: tensor products create systematic non-cancellation phenomena and many zero-divisors. The key invariant is the balance of the directed graph associated with a natural basis. We prove that, for non-degenerate evolution algebras, this balance is independent of the chosen natural basis. We then show that balance controls cancellation after tensoring: indecomposable factors of balance 11 cancel, whereas factors of larger balance produce zero-divisor relations under mild hypotheses. Finally, we analyze the subring generated by cyclic evolution algebras and prove the predicted zero-divisor criterion for all finite direct sums of cyclic algebras.

1. Introduction

Evolution algebras form a class of commutative, generally non-associative algebras designed to encode non-Mendelian inheritance. Their defining feature is the existence of a natural basis B={e1,…,en}B=\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}\} in which mixed products vanish, ei​ej=0e_{i}e_{j}=0 for i≠ji\neq j. Consequently, the whole multiplication is encoded by the squares of the basis elements, or equivalently by a single structure matrix. This places evolution algebras at the intersection of non-associative algebra, weighted directed graphs, and Markov-chain dynamics [12, 11, 8, 9].

A central problem in the theory is classification, usually understood as the determination of the isomorphism types of indecomposable evolution algebras. Although low-dimensional classifications are known [4], the case-by-case approach quickly becomes unfeasible. In fact, realization results show that every finite group occurs as the full automorphism group of a non-degenerate, finite-dimensional indecomposable evolution algebra [6, 7]. Thus, the classification problem for evolution algebras is at least as complicated as the classification of finite groups, and cannot reasonably be expected to admit a simple complete invariant. This obstruction motivates the categorical viewpoint adopted in this paper: we study how evolution algebras combine, rather than trying to enumerate them one by one.

The category Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} of finite-dimensional non-degenerate evolution algebras over a field 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} is closed under two operations: the direct sum ⊕\oplus, which is indeed the categorical product in Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}, and the tensor product ⊗\otimes. Both are symmetric monoidal, and ⊗\otimes is distributive with respect to ⊕\oplus, see Section 4. This is exactly the input needed to form a Grothendieck ring 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), in which isomorphism classes are added by ⊕\oplus and multiplied by ⊗\otimes, see Section 5.

The pay-off is a change of perspective on what “classification” should mean. As an abelian group, (𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd),+)(\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}),+) is free on the isomorphism classes of non-degenerate indecomposable algebras, so describing its additive generators is just the original, intractable problem in disguise. As a ring, however, 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is “smaller”; there exist indecomposable non-degenerate evolution algebras which are tensorially decomposable, see Section 12, and moreover 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) has many zero-divisors, see Theorem A below. Therefore, we propose to classify ring generators of 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}): these are some of the additive generators but also exploit the multiplication, and there are far fewer of them.

Understanding 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) as a ring, rather than merely as an abelian group, reframes the classification of evolution algebras. A description of its ring generators and of its ideal of zero-divisors would, in particular, open the door to a probabilistic classification (asking for the typical behaviour of a random evolution algebra rather than a complete list), and to the study of growth, that is, the asymptotics of the number of indecomposables of a given dimension.

We conclude this section by proving that the ring 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) contains zero-divisors. This introductory argument also serves as a preview of the methods developed in the sequel, where the relevant constructions and proofs are given in full detail. The central invariant in the arguments is the balance of the directed graph associated with a natural basis. While the graph itself may depend on the chosen basis, its balance does not: for non-degenerate evolution algebras it is an intrinsic invariant (Theorem 6.1).

Theorem A.

Let XX be a finite dimensional non-degenerate evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra, and let

X=⨁j=1rXjX=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{r}X_{j}

be its optimal direct-sum decomposition into indecomposable evolution ideals. Assume each XjX_{j} has balance

b⁡(Xj)>1.\operatorname{b}(X_{j})>1.

Then XX gives rise to a zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), that is, there exist non-degenerate finite-dimensional evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras AA and BB such that A⊗X≅B⊗XA\otimes X\cong B\otimes X, while A≇BA\not\cong B.

Proof.

Observe that since pj>1p_{j}>1, Uj≇VjU_{j}\not\cong V_{j} as they have different optimal direct-sum decomposition into indecomposable evolution ideals. But the pjp_{j}-isomorphism in Example 7.8 shows UjΦ=VjU_{j}^{\Phi}=V_{j}, so by Theorem 8.2 one has Uj⊗Cpj≅Vj⊗CpjU_{j}\otimes C_{p_{j}}\cong V_{j}\otimes C_{p_{j}} relative to CpjC_{p_{j}}. Applying Theorem 10.4 with D=XjD=X_{j} gives Uj⊗Xj≅Vj⊗XjU_{j}\otimes X_{j}\cong V_{j}\otimes X_{j}, so the isomorphism class of XjX_{j}, namely [Xj][X_{j}], is a zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) since

[Xj]​([Cpj]−pj​[𝕂])=0.[X_{j}]([C_{p_{j}}]-p_{j}[{\mathbb{K}}])=0.

Define q=rad⁡(∏j=1rpj)q=\operatorname{rad}(\prod_{j=1}^{r}p_{j}), that is, qq is the largest square-free integer that divides ∏j=1rpj\prod_{j=1}^{r}p_{j}, and let q=q1​…​qsq=q_{1}\ldots q_{s} be its prime factorization. Therefore, for each jj there exists some qiq_{i} such that pj=qip_{j}=q_{i} and [Xj]​([Cqi]−qi​[𝕂])=0,[X_{j}]([C_{q_{i}}]-q_{i}[{\mathbb{K}}])=0, and

[X]​(∏i=1s([Cqi]−qi​[𝕂]))\displaystyle[X]\big(\prod_{i=1}^{s}([C_{q_{i}}]-q_{i}[{\mathbb{K}}])\big) =(∑j=1r[Xj])​(∏i=1s([Cqi]−qi​[𝕂]))\displaystyle=(\sum_{j=1}^{r}[X_{j}])\big(\prod_{i=1}^{s}([C_{q_{i}}]-q_{i}[{\mathbb{K}}])\big)
=∑j=1r[Xj]​(∏i=1s([Cqi]−qi​[𝕂]))\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{r}[X_{j}]\big(\prod_{i=1}^{s}([C_{q_{i}}]-q_{i}[{\mathbb{K}}])\big)
=0\displaystyle=0

∏i=1s([Cqi]−qi​[𝕂])=[A]−[B]\prod_{i=1}^{s}([C_{q_{i}}]-q_{i}[{\mathbb{K}}])=[A]-[B]

thus X⊗A≅X⊗BX\otimes A\cong X\otimes B. Notice that A≇BA\not\cong B, or equivalently [A]−[B]≠0,[A]-[B]\neq 0, since by repeated use of Example 12.2 we get that AA and BB have different optimal direct-sum decomposition into indecomposable evolution ideals. In particular AA contains a summand of type Cq≅⊗i=1sCqiC_{q}\cong{\otimes}_{i=1}^{s}C_{q_{i}} while BB does not. ∎

While we do not have a complete description of all zero-divisors in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), the following conjecture appears to be well motivated.

Conjecture 1.1.

An evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra is a zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) if and only if each of its indecomposable direct summands has balance greater than 11.

Remark 1.2.

Notice that Lemma 5.3 allows one to combine the zero-divisor relations associated with the indecomposable summands into a single relation for their direct sum. This establishes precisely the sufficiency direction of Conjecture 1.1, which Theorem A already proves for arbitrary direct sums.

By contrast, Lemma 5.3 does not reduce the necessity direction to the indecomposable case. There is no converse “de-combination” principle: a direct sum containing both a balance-11 summand and summands of balance greater than 11 could, a priori, be a zero-divisor for reasons that are not detected at the level of the individual summands. Therefore, Conjecture 1.1 cannot, on the basis of Lemma 5.3, be reduced to the indecomposable case.

2. Graphs and the balance invariant

In this section we briefly recall the basics in Graph Theory we use in the following sections. All graphs in this paper are directed, and we follow the conventions of [8, 9, 10].

Definition 2.1.

A graph is a pair Γ=(V,E)\Gamma=(V,E) consisting of a finite set of vertices VV and a set of edges (or arrows) E⊆V×VE\subseteq V\times V.

Definition 2.2.

A path in Γ\Gamma is a sequence

γ=(v0,e1,v1,…,vn−1,en,vn),n≥0,\gamma=(v_{0},e_{1},v_{1},\dots,v_{n-1},e_{n},v_{n}),\qquad n\geq 0,

with v0,…,vn∈Vv_{0},\dots,v_{n}\in V and e1,…,en∈Ee_{1},\dots,e_{n}\in E such that, for each i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, either ei=(vi−1,vi)e_{i}=(v_{i-1},v_{i}) (the edge is traversed forwards) or ei=(vi,vi−1)e_{i}=(v_{i},v_{i-1}) (traversed backwards). A (non-simple) cycle is a path with v0=vnv_{0}=v_{n}. The balance of γ\gamma is the integer

b⁡(γ)=#⁡{i:ei=(vi−1,vi)}−#⁡{i:ei=(vi,vi−1)},\operatorname{b}(\gamma)=\#\{\,i:e_{i}=(v_{i-1},v_{i})\,\}-\#\{\,i:e_{i}=(v_{i},v_{i-1})\,\},

that is, +1+1 for each edge traversed in the “right” direction (from v0v_{0} towards vnv_{n}) and −1-1 for each edge traversed in the “wrong” direction, summed over ii.

Remark 2.3.

Observe that balance behaves naturally with respect to the two elementary operations on paths: it is additive under concatenation and changes sign under reversal. Thus, if α\alpha and β\beta are paths in Γ\Gamma with the same final vertex, then α⋆β−1\alpha\star\beta^{-1} is a well-defined path, where ⋆\star denotes concatenation and β−1\beta^{-1} is the path β\beta traversed in the opposite direction. Hence

b⁡(α⋆β−1)=b⁡(α)+b⁡(β−1)=b⁡(α)−b⁡(β).\operatorname{b}(\alpha\star\beta^{-1})=\operatorname{b}(\alpha)+\operatorname{b}(\beta^{-1})=\operatorname{b}(\alpha)-\operatorname{b}(\beta).
Definition 2.4.

The balance of Γ\Gamma is the greatest common divisor of the absolute values of the balances of its cycles,

b⁡(Γ)=gcd⁡{|b⁡(γ)|:γ​ a cycle in ​Γ}.\operatorname{b}(\Gamma)=\gcd\{\,|\operatorname{b}(\gamma)|:\gamma\text{ a cycle in }\Gamma\,\}.
Remark 2.5.

The notions of balance of a path and of a graph introduced here agree with those in [8, 9] and constitute the terminology commonly used in the context of evolution algebras. They also coincide with the notions of weight introduced by Chen and Chen in [5].

Definition 2.6.

The indegree and outdegree of a vertex v∈Vv\in V are

deg−⁡(v)=#⁡{w∈V:(w,v)∈E},deg+⁡(v)=#⁡{w∈V:(v,w)∈E}.\deg^{-}(v)=\#\{\,w\in V:(w,v)\in E\,\},\qquad\deg^{+}(v)=\#\{\,w\in V:(v,w)\in E\,\}.

The vertex vv is a source if deg−⁡(v)=0\deg^{-}(v)=0 and a sink if deg+⁡(v)=0\deg^{+}(v)=0. The graph Γ\Gamma is connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected, that is, if for every v,w∈Vv,w\in V there is a path from vv to ww.

The following results characterize the balance of connected graphs.

Lemma 2.7.

Let Γ=(V,E)\Gamma=(V,E) be a connected graph with b⁡(Γ)=d\operatorname{b}(\Gamma)=d. Then, for every v0∈Vv_{0}\in V, Γ\Gamma contains a cycle γ\gamma with base point v0v_{0} and b⁡(γ)=d\operatorname{b}(\gamma)=d.

Proof.

By definition b⁡(Γ)=gcd⁡{|b⁡(γ)|:γ​ a cycle}=d\operatorname{b}(\Gamma)=\gcd\{\,|\operatorname{b}(\gamma)|:\gamma\text{ a cycle}\,\}=d, so by Bézout’s identity, there are cycles γ1,…,γr\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{r} and integers α1,…,αr\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r} with ∑j=1rαj​b⁡(γj)=d\sum_{j=1}^{r}\alpha_{j}\,\operatorname{b}(\gamma_{j})=d. Fix the base point v0v_{0}. Since Γ\Gamma is connected, for each j≥1j\geq 1, there is a path βj\beta_{j} from v0v_{0} to the base point of γj\gamma_{j}. Concatenating βj\beta_{j}, traversing each γj\gamma_{j} exactly |αj||\alpha_{j}| times in the direction sg⁡(αj)\operatorname{sg}(\alpha_{j}) and returning along βj−1\beta_{j}^{-1} for each j≥1j\geq 1, namely

γ=⋆j=1r(βj⋆γjαj⋆βj−1),\gamma=\operatornamewithlimits{\star}_{j=1}^{r}\bigl(\beta_{j}\star\gamma_{j}^{\alpha_{j}}\star\beta_{j}^{-1}\bigr),

gives a cycle based at v0v_{0}. Applying Remark 2.3 yields

b⁡(γ)=∑j=1r(b⁡(βj)+αj​b⁡(γj)−b⁡(βj))=∑j=1rαj​b⁡(γj)=d.∎\operatorname{b}(\gamma)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\big(\operatorname{b}(\beta_{j})+\alpha_{j}\operatorname{b}(\gamma_{j})-\operatorname{b}(\beta_{j})\big)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\alpha_{j}\operatorname{b}(\gamma_{j})=d.\qed
Lemma 2.8.

Let Γ=(V,E)\Gamma=(V,E) be a connected graph with no sinks. Then b⁡(Γ)≥1\operatorname{b}(\Gamma)\geq 1, and for any positive integer dd the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    dd divides b⁡(Γ)\operatorname{b}(\Gamma).

  2. (ii)

    There exists a surjective map

    hd:V⟶ℤ/d,h_{d}\colon V\longrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}/d,

    such that if (v,w)∈E(v,w)\in E then hd​(w)=hd​(v)+1(modd).h_{d}(w)=h_{d}(v)+1\pmod{d}.

Proof.

Since Γ\Gamma has no sink, every vertex has out-degree ≥1\geq 1, and a finite graph with this property contains a cycle, of balance equal to its length, so b⁡(Γ)≥1\operatorname{b}(\Gamma)\geq 1.

Fix now an integer d>0.d>0.

We assume first that dd divides b⁡(Γ)\operatorname{b}(\Gamma). Choose a vertex v0v_{0}, and define hd​(v0)=0h_{d}(v_{0})=0. For any vertex vv, choose a path γ\gamma from v0v_{0} to vv and set hd​(v)=b⁡(γ)moddh_{d}(v)=\operatorname{b}(\gamma)\bmod d. This is well defined: a second path γ′\gamma^{\prime} gives a cycle γ−γ′\gamma-\gamma^{\prime}, whose balance is divisible by b⁡(Γ)\operatorname{b}(\Gamma) and hence by dd, so b⁡(γ)≡b⁡(γ′)(modd)\operatorname{b}(\gamma)\equiv\operatorname{b}(\gamma^{\prime})\pmod{d}. Appending an edge (v,w)∈E(v,w)\in E to the path γ\gamma gives a path from v0v_{0} to ww that raises balance by 11, giving hd​(w)=hd​(v)+1h_{d}(w)=h_{d}(v)+1. Finally, since Γ\Gamma has no sinks it contains a directed cycle ZZ of some length LL; its balance is LL, so d​∣b⁡(Γ)∣​Ld\mid\operatorname{b}(\Gamma)\mid L and L≥dL\geq d. Traversing ZZ, consecutive vertices have consecutive heights hd​(u0)+k(modd)h_{d}(u_{0})+k\pmod{d}, and L≥dL\geq d forces these to exhaust ℤ/d{\mathbb{Z}}/d; hence hdh_{d} is surjective.

Now, assume there exists hd:V→ℤ/dh_{d}\colon V\to{\mathbb{Z}}/d such that if (v,w)∈E(v,w)\in E then hd​(w)=hd​(v)+1(modd).h_{d}(w)=h_{d}(v)+1\pmod{d}. For any given vertex v0∈Vv_{0}\in V traversing the directed cycle with base point v0v_{0} given by Lemma 2.7 shows that hd​(v0)=hd​(v0)+b⁡(Γ)(modd),h_{d}(v_{0})=h_{d}(v_{0})+\operatorname{b}(\Gamma)\pmod{d}, that holds only if b⁡(Γ)=0(modd),\operatorname{b}(\Gamma)=0\pmod{d}, that is, if dd divides b⁡(Γ).\operatorname{b}(\Gamma). ∎

3. Basic definitions on evolution algebras

In this section, we establish the notation and recall the basic definitions concerning evolution algebras that are used throughout the paper. Unless stated otherwise, 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} denotes a field, and all 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras are assumed to be finite-dimensional.

Definition 3.1.

A 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra XX is an evolution algebra if it admits a basis B={e1,…,en}B=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\}, called a natural basis, such that ei​ej=0e_{i}\,e_{j}=0 whenever i≠ji\neq j.

Relative to such a basis the products of the basis elements with themselves are recorded by scalars wi​k∈𝕂w_{ik}\in{\mathbb{K}} via

ei 2=∑k=1nwi​k​ek,e_{i}^{\,2}\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{n}w_{ik}\,e_{k},

and the matrix MB​(X)=(wi​k)M_{B}(X)=(w_{ik}) is the structure matrix of XX relative to BB.

Evolution algebras are commutative because the product of distinct basis vectors is zero. However, they are generally neither associative nor power-associative. Once a natural basis BB is fixed, the algebra is completely determined by its structure matrix MB​(X)=(wi​k)M_{B}(X)=(w_{ik}). Geometrically and biologically, this structure carries two primary interpretations [11]: in genetics, each generator eie_{i} represents a type and ei2e_{i}^{2} its offspring distribution, while the Markov-chain interpretation takes the wi​kw_{ik} to be transition weights from state ii to state kk.

Remark 3.2.

The natural basis is not unique, and neither is the structure matrix: a given evolution algebra can carry several genuinely different natural bases. This non-uniqueness is the source of most of the subtlety in the theory and is precisely what the rigidified category of Section 7 is designed to control.

Definition 3.3.

An evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra XX is non-degenerate if it admits a natural basis B={e1,…,en}B=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\} such that ei2≠0e_{i}^{2}\neq 0 for i=1,…,n.i=1,\ldots,n.

Remark 3.4.

The property of being non-degenerate is independent of the chosen basis. Indeed, according to [3, Corollary 2.19], an evolution algebra XX is non-degenerate if and only if

Ann⁡(X)={x∈X:x​X=0}=0.\operatorname{Ann}(X)=\{x\in X:xX=0\}=0.
Definition 3.5.

Let XX be an evolution algebra with natural basis B={e1,…,en}B=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\} and structure matrix (wi​k)(w_{ik}). The associated graph Γ⁡(X,B)\Gamma(X,B) is defined as the graph on the vertex set {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} that has an edge (i,k)(i,k) whenever wi​k≠0w_{ik}\neq 0 [8, 9].

Many algebraic features of XX (nilpotency, simplicity, ideals) are visible in Γ⁡(X,B)\Gamma(X,B). However, the correspondence between evolution algebras and their associated graphs is neither bijective nor functorial: it depends on the chosen natural basis (Remark 3.2), and a homomorphism of evolution algebras need not rescale the prescribed natural bases, hence need not induce a morphism of graphs. Nevertheless, we prove in Section 6 that the balance of the graph Γ⁡(X,B)\Gamma(X,B) is an intrinsic invariant of XX that does not depend on the chosen natural basis BB if XX is non-degenerate.

4. Monoidal structure on Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}

Recall the category Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} is defined as the full subcategory of the category of 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras which is spanned by finite-dimensional non-degenerate evolution algebras. The category Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} is closed under two operations:

  • •

    The direct sum X⊕YX\oplus Y: It is the categorical product in Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}. Indeed, given XX, and YY non-degenerate evolution algebras with natural basis BB and B′B^{\prime} respectively, then B⊕{0}⊔{0}⊕B′B\oplus\{0\}\sqcup\{0\}\oplus B^{\prime} is a natural basis of X⊕YX\oplus Y, whose structure matrix is the block diagonal matrix of those of XX and YY. Moreover, since multiplication in X⊕YX\oplus Y is component wise, the square of every element in B⊕{0}⊔{0}⊕B′B\oplus\{0\}\sqcup\{0\}\oplus B^{\prime} is non trivial, that is X⊕YX\oplus Y is non-degenerate. Moreover, X⊕YX\oplus Y is the categorical product: the projections πX:X⊕Y→X\pi_{X}\colon X\oplus Y\to X and πY:X⊕Y→Y\pi_{Y}\colon X\oplus Y\to Y are homomorphisms of evolution algebras, and for any non-degenerate evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra ZZ with homomorphisms f:Z→Xf\colon Z\to X and g:Z→Yg\colon Z\to Y, the map z↦(f⁡(z),g⁡(z))z\mapsto(f(z),g(z)) is the unique homomorphism Z→X⊕YZ\to X\oplus Y with πX∘(f,g)=f\pi_{X}\circ(f,g)=f and πY∘(f,g)=g\pi_{Y}\circ(f,g)=g; it is multiplicative because products across the two blocks vanish.

    Every non-degenerate evolution algebra admits a unique optimal direct-sum decomposition into indecomposable evolution ideals [3, Theorem 5.11]. In other words, every non-degenerate evolution algebra decomposes in a unique way as a direct sum of indecomposable evolution algebras. Finally, the zero algebra 00 is non-degenerate evolution algebra since it admits an empty natural basis, and it is a unit for this operation.

  • •

    The tensor product X⊗YX\otimes Y: Let XX and YY be evolution algebras over a field 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}, each endowed with natural bases B={ei}i∈IB=\{e_{i}\}_{i\in I} and B′={fj}j∈JB^{\prime}=\{f_{j}\}_{j\in J} respectively. It is well known, e.g. [2, Theorem 3.2], that the tensor product algebra X⊗YX\otimes Y admits a natural basis given by B⊗B′={ei⊗fj}(i,j)∈I×JB\otimes B^{\prime}=\{e_{i}\otimes f_{j}\}_{(i,j)\in I\times J}, with multiplication determined by

    (ei⊗fj)2=ei2⊗fj2,(ei⊗fj)​(ei′⊗fj′)=0​ for ​(i,j)≠(i′,j′).(e_{i}\otimes f_{j})^{2}=e_{i}^{2}\otimes f_{j}^{2},\quad(e_{i}\otimes f_{j})(e_{i^{\prime}}\otimes f_{j^{\prime}})=0\text{ for }(i,j)\neq(i^{\prime},j^{\prime}).

    Hence X⊗YX\otimes Y is itself an evolution algebra, its structure matrix is the Kronecker product of the structure matrices of XX and YY [2, Remark 3.3]. Moreover, if both XX and YY are non-degenerate, then for every basis element ei⊗fje_{i}\otimes f_{j} one has

    (ei⊗fj)2=ei2⊗fj2≠0,(e_{i}\otimes f_{j})^{2}=e_{i}^{2}\otimes f_{j}^{2}\neq 0,

    since both tensor factors are nonzero, and X⊗YX\otimes Y is again non-degenerate [2, Lemma 3.8]. Therefore, the class of non-degenerate evolution algebras is closed under tensor products. The one-dimensional algebra 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}, acts as a unit for this operation.

Since the usual direct sum and tensor product of 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras are associative and symmetric up to canonical isomorphism, it follows that the category Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} inherits a symmetric monoidal structure from the ambient category of 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras when considering these two operations. This is made explicit in the following statement.

Proposition 4.1.

(Evol𝕂nd,⊕,0)(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}},\oplus,0) and (Evol𝕂nd,⊗,𝕂)(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}},\otimes,{\mathbb{K}}) are symmetric monoidal categories, and ⊗\otimes is distributive with respect to ⊕\oplus:

X⊗(Y⊕Z)≅(X⊗Y)⊕(X⊗Z).X\otimes(Y\oplus Z)\;\cong\;(X\otimes Y)\oplus(X\otimes Z).
Proof.

The symmetric monoidal structures are inherited from the ambient category of 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras, as noted above; only the distributivity isomorphism requires comment. Let BXB_{X}, BYB_{Y}, BZB_{Z} be natural bases of XX, YY, ZZ. On the one hand, Y⊕ZY\oplus Z has natural basis BY⊔BZB_{Y}\sqcup B_{Z}, so X⊗(Y⊕Z)X\otimes(Y\oplus Z) has natural basis

BX⊗(BY⊔BZ)=(BX⊗BY)⊔(BX⊗BZ).B_{X}\otimes(B_{Y}\sqcup B_{Z})=(B_{X}\otimes B_{Y})\sqcup(B_{X}\otimes B_{Z}).

On the other hand, this is precisely the natural basis of (X⊗Y)⊕(X⊗Z)(X\otimes Y)\oplus(X\otimes Z). The linear bijection matching e⊗fe\otimes f to itself under this identification preserves squares, since (e⊗f)2=e2⊗f2(e\otimes f)^{2}=e^{2}\otimes f^{2} in both algebras and products of distinct natural basis vectors vanish on both sides; hence it is an isomorphism of evolution algebras. ∎

The distributivity in Proposition 4.1 is exactly the compatibility one needs between an “addition” and a “multiplication” to form a ring out of isomorphism classes, which is the subject of the next section.

5. The Grothendieck ring of Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}

In this section we introduce 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), the Grothendieck ring of finite-dimensional non-degenerate evolution algebras and some of its basic properties.

Write [X][X] for the isomorphism class of an evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra XX .

Definition 5.1.

The Grothendieck ring of Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} is the ring

𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)=(G,+,⋅)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}})=(G,+,\cdot)

generated by the symbols [X][X], for XX an object in Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}, subject to the relations

(1) [X]=[Y]\displaystyle[X]=[Y] ⇔X≅Y,\displaystyle\iff X\cong Y,
(2) [X]+[Y]\displaystyle[X]+[Y] =[X⊕Y],\displaystyle=[X\oplus Y],
(3) [X]−[Y]=[Z]\displaystyle[X]-[Y]=[Z] ⇔[X]=[Z⊕Y],\displaystyle\iff[X]=[Z\oplus Y],
(4) [X]⋅[Y]\displaystyle[X]\cdot[Y] =[X⊗Y].\displaystyle=[X\otimes Y].

Relations (2)–(3) record the additive (group completion) structure coming from ⊕\oplus, while (4) introduces the multiplication coming from ⊗\otimes; that the latter is well defined and distributes over the former is guaranteed by Proposition 4.1. This construction is well defined. By [3, Theorem 5.11] the commutative monoid ({[X]},⊕)(\{[X]\},\oplus) of isomorphism classes is free on the indecomposables, hence cancellative, so its group completion is the free abelian group on the indecomposables and the natural map into it is injective. The product ⊗\otimes respects isomorphism and distributes over ⊕\oplus by Proposition 4.1, so it descends to a well-defined, commutative, distributive multiplication on this group completion. In particular, collecting the positive and negative coefficients of a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-combination ∑kck​[Yk]\sum_{k}c_{k}[Y_{k}] as [A]−[B][A]-[B], with A=⨁ck>0Yk⊕ckA=\bigoplus_{c_{k}>0}Y_{k}^{\oplus c_{k}} and B=⨁ck<0Yk⊕(−ck)B=\bigoplus_{c_{k}<0}Y_{k}^{\oplus(-c_{k})}, produces genuine non-degenerate algebras, since Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} is closed under ⊕\oplus (Section 4). This is what Lemma 5.3 and Theorem A use when reading off X⊗A≅X⊗BX\otimes A\cong X\otimes B.

Remark 5.2.

The Grothendieck ring 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is a commutative ring with unity. As it was mentioned in the previous section, the additive zero is the class of the trivial (zero) evolution algebra,

0=[0],[X]+0=[X⊕0]=[X],0=[0],\qquad[X]+0=[X\oplus 0]=[X],

while multiplicative unit is the class of the one-dimensional evolution algebra 𝕂=𝕂​{e}{\mathbb{K}}={\mathbb{K}}\{e\}, with e2=ee^{2}=e, taken with the natural basis {e}\{e\},

1=[𝕂],[X]⋅1=[X]⋅[𝕂]=[X⊗𝕂]=[X],1=[{\mathbb{K}}],\qquad[X]\cdot 1=[X]\cdot[{\mathbb{K}}]=[X\otimes{\mathbb{K}}]=[X],

the latter because 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} is the unit for ⊗\otimes (Proposition 4.1).

As an abelian group, 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is free. Indeed, since every finite-dimensional non-degenerate evolution algebra decomposes in a unique way as a direct sum of indecomposable evolution algebras [3, Theorem 5.11], so the isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional indecomposables non-degenerate evolution algebras form a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-basis:

(𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd),+)=⨁[X]​indecomp.ℤ⁡[X].(\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}),+)\;=\;\bigoplus_{[X]\ \text{indecomp.}}{\mathbb{Z}}\,[X].

This group is huge, and listing a set of additive generators is literally the wild classification problem from the introduction.

As a ring, by contrast, 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is generated by far fewer elements, because the product (4) imposes relations, in particular many zero-divisors, among the additive generators. Concretely, two phenomena reduce the number of generators one must list.

(a) Indecomposable products are not needed as ring generators. There exist indecomposable non-degenerate evolution algebras XX and YY such that the tensor product X⊗YX\otimes Y is again indecomposable (see Theorem 12.4). In this case, the three classes [X][X], [Y][Y] and [X⊗Y][X\otimes Y] are distinct additive basis elements and would all have to be recorded. However, as ring elements, [X⊗Y]=[X]​[Y][X\otimes Y]=[X][Y] by (4), so once [X][X] and [Y][Y] are known, the class [X⊗Y][X\otimes Y] is determined, and need not be listed separately as a generator.

(b) Non-cancellation phenomena produce zero-divisors. As we show in the following pages, there exist non-degenerate evolution algebras XX, YY, and ZZ such that

X⊗Y≅X⊗Zeven thoughY≇Z.X\otimes Y\cong X\otimes Z\qquad\text{even though}\qquad Y\not\cong Z.

In the Grothendieck ring 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), this relation becomes

[X]​([Y]−[Z])=0with[Y]−[Z]≠0,[X]\bigl([Y]-[Z]\bigr)=0\qquad\text{with}\qquad[Y]-[Z]\neq 0,

which proves that [X][X] is a zero-divisor. Consequently, the presence of these relations implies that 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is not a free ring. This imposes constraints on the generators: we do not need to record all products individually, as many are already determined by these algebraic dependencies.

To conclude this section, we illustrate how algebraic manipulations in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) give rise to identities that may be of independent interest, as they exhibit further instances of non-cancellation phenomena.

Lemma 5.3.

Let AiA_{i}, BiB_{i} and DiD_{i}, i=1,2,i=1,2, be non-degenerate evolution algebras. Suppose Ai⊗Di≅Bi⊗DiA_{i}\otimes D_{i}\cong B_{i}\otimes D_{i} for i=1,2i=1,2. Then

(A1⊗A2⊕B1⊗B2)⊗(D1⊕D2)≅(A1⊗B2⊕B1⊗A2)⊗(D1⊕D2).(A_{1}\otimes A_{2}\;\oplus\;B_{1}\otimes B_{2})\otimes(D_{1}\oplus D_{2})\;\cong\;(A_{1}\otimes B_{2}\;\oplus\;B_{1}\otimes A_{2})\otimes(D_{1}\oplus D_{2}).
Proof.

In 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) the hypotheses Ai⊗Di≅Bi⊗DiA_{i}\otimes D_{i}\cong B_{i}\otimes D_{i} read

([Ai]−[Bi])​[Di]=0(i=1,2).([A_{i}]-[B_{i}])\,[D_{i}]=0\qquad(i=1,2).

Therefore

P:=([A1]−[B1])​([A2]−[B2])​([D1]+[D2]).P:=([A_{1}]-[B_{1}])\,([A_{2}]-[B_{2}])\,\bigl([D_{1}]+[D_{2}]\bigr).

On the one hand, multiplying out and using (2)–(4),

P=[(A1⊗A2)⊕(B1⊗B2)]​[D1⊕D2]−[(A1⊗B2)⊕(B1⊗A2)]​[D1⊕D2],\begin{split}P&=\bigl[(A_{1}\otimes A_{2})\oplus(B_{1}\otimes B_{2})\bigr]\bigl[D_{1}\oplus D_{2}\bigr]\\ &\quad-\bigl[(A_{1}\otimes B_{2})\oplus(B_{1}\otimes A_{2})\bigr]\bigl[D_{1}\oplus D_{2}\bigr],\end{split}

which is exactly the difference of the classes of the two sides of the claimed isomorphism. On the other hand, expanding PP over [D1]+[D2][D_{1}]+[D_{2}] and using commutativity of 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}),

P=([A2]−[B2])​([A1]−[B1])​[D1]⏟=0+([A1]−[B1])​([A2]−[B2])​[D2]⏟=0=0,P=([A_{2}]-[B_{2}])\,\underbrace{([A_{1}]-[B_{1}])[D_{1}]}_{=0}+([A_{1}]-[B_{1}])\,\underbrace{([A_{2}]-[B_{2}])[D_{2}]}_{=0}=0,

each summand vanishing by the hypotheses. Hence the difference of the two classes is 00, that is, they are equal; since ⊕\oplus-decomposition into indecomposables is essentially unique, equal classes come from isomorphic algebras, which is the stated isomorphism. ∎

6. Balance of non-degenerate algebras is an invariant

In the following sections we show that whether or not an indecomposable object XX in Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} gives rise to a zero divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is controlled by the balance of XX. But a non-degenerate evolution algebra XX can carry genuinely different natural bases BB with different associated graphs (Remark 3.2), thus the quantity b⁡(Γ⁡(X,B))\operatorname{b}(\Gamma(X,B)) is a priori basis-dependent. In this section we show that is not the case.

Theorem 6.1.

Let A≠0A\neq 0 be a finite-dimensional non-degenerate evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra. Then b⁡(Γ⁡(A,B))\operatorname{b}(\Gamma(A,B)) does not depend on the chosen natural basis BB of AA.

Proof.

Since AA is non-degenerate, then b2≠0b^{2}\neq 0 for all b∈B,b\in B, and every vertex of Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) has at least one outgoing arrow; equivalently, Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) has no sinks.

Since the graph Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) is finite, starting at any vertex and successively following an outgoing arrow eventually produces a repeated vertex. Thus Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) contains a directed cycle, and in particular, b⁡(Γ⁡(A,B))\operatorname{b}(\Gamma(A,B)) is a well-defined positive integer.

We now use the canonical evolution rank-one decomposition of AA: by [1, Theorem 2.11], there is a decomposition

(5) A=E1⊕⋯⊕ErA=E_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus E_{r}

such that

dimEi2=1,andEi​Ej=0,dim(Ei2+Ej2)=2(i≠j).\dim E_{i}^{2}=1,\qquad\text{and}\qquad E_{i}E_{j}=0,\quad\dim(E_{i}^{2}+E_{j}^{2})=2\quad(i\neq j).

Because AA is non-degenerate, the decomposition given in Equation (5) is unique, up to a permutation of its summands. Moreover, the proof of [1, Theorem 2.11, p. 165] also shows that any natural basis BB of AA admits a partition

(6) B=B1∪˙⋯∪˙BrB=B_{1}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}\cdots\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}B_{r}

such that BiB_{i} is a basis of EiE_{i}.

We are defining a graph Γ¯​(A)\overline{\Gamma}(A) associated to the decomposition given in Equation (5). For each ii, choose a nonzero vector qi∈Ei2.q_{i}\in E_{i}^{2}. Since Equation (5) holds, there are uniquely determined vectors qi​j∈Ejq_{ij}\in E_{j} such that

qi=qi​1+⋯+qi​r.q_{i}=q_{i1}+\cdots+q_{ir}.

Then Γ¯​(A)\overline{\Gamma}(A) is the graph whose vertices are E1,…,Er,E_{1},\dots,E_{r}, and whose edges are determined by

(Ei,Ej)∈Γ¯(A)⟺qi​j≠0.(E_{i},E_{j})\in\overline{\Gamma}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad q_{ij}\neq 0.

This definition of Γ¯​(A)\overline{\Gamma}(A) is independent of the choice of the nonzero generator qi∈Ei2q_{i}\in E_{i}^{2}, because replacing qiq_{i} by a nonzero scalar multiple (recall that dimEi2=1\dim E_{i}^{2}=1) does not change which components qi​jq_{ij} vanish. The uniqueness clause in [1, Theorem 2.11] therefore implies that Γ¯​(A)\overline{\Gamma}(A) is intrinsic to AA, up to relabelling its vertices.

e2=λe​qi=λe​(qi​1+⋯+qi​r).e^{2}=\lambda_{e}q_{i}=\lambda_{e}(q_{i1}+\cdots+q_{ir}).

For every pair i,ji,j, define

Si​j​(B)={f∈Bj:the coefficient of f in qi​j is nonzero}.S_{ij}(B)=\left\{f\in B_{j}:\text{the coefficient of $f$ in $q_{ij}$ is nonzero}\right\}.

Thus all vertices belonging to the same block BiB_{i} have the same successors inside every block BjB_{j}. In other words, the map given at level of vertices by

Remark 6.2.

Since for any given finite-dimensional non-degenerate evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra A≠0A\neq 0, the value b⁡(Γ⁡(A,B))\operatorname{b}(\Gamma(A,B)) does not depend on the chosen natural basis BB of AA, we shall simply write b⁡(A)\operatorname{b}(A). In particular b⁡(A)\operatorname{b}(A) is well defined for every non-degenerate AA.

7. The rigidified category NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}

As it was mentioned in Section 3, the main difficulty when working with evolution algebras is that algebra homomorphisms ignore the natural basis. We therefore work in a category in which the natural basis, or rather the resulting decomposition into lines, is part of the structure that morphisms must preserve.

Definition 7.1.

The category of natural evolution algebras over 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} is the category whose objects and morphisms are:

Objects:

A natural evolution algebra is a non-degenerate evolution algebra XX, together with a fixed decomposition

X=⨁i=1nAi,Ai​Aj=0​(i≠j),dim𝕂Ai=1,X=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}A_{i},\qquad A_{i}A_{j}=0\ (i\neq j),\qquad\dim_{\mathbb{K}}A_{i}=1,

into one-dimensional subspaces with pairwise trivial products.

Morphisms:

A morphism in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} is a 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra homomorphism that preserves the decomposition, that is, an algebra morphism f:⨁iAi→⨁jBjf\colon\bigoplus_{i}A_{i}\to\bigoplus_{j}B_{j} such that each line is sent into a line,

f⁡(Ai)⊆Bjfor some ​j.f(A_{i})\subseteq B_{j}\quad\text{for some }j.

Equivalently, ff comes with a map of index sets f^:I→J\hat{f}\colon I\to J with

f⁡(Ai)⊆Bf^​(i)(i∈I).f(A_{i})\subseteq B_{\hat{f}(i)}\qquad(i\in I).

We further require that no line is annihilated: f⁡(Ai)≠0f(A_{i})\neq 0 for every ii (equivalently, ff restricts to a linear isomorphism Ai→≅Bf^​(i)A_{i}\xrightarrow{\cong}B_{\hat{f}(i)}), so that the index map f^\hat{f} is well defined.

Remark 7.2.

Observe that there is a forgetful functor

NEvol𝕂nd↝Evol𝕂nd.\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}\rightsquigarrow\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}.

given by forgetting the natural decomposition. This is a faithful functor which is clearly not an embedding: A single evolution algebra XX may carry two different natural bases B1,B2B_{1},B_{2}, giving two different objects

X1=⨁b∈B1𝕂⁡{b},X2=⨁b∈B2𝕂⁡{b}X_{1}=\bigoplus_{b\in B_{1}}{\mathbb{K}}\{b\},\qquad X_{2}=\bigoplus_{b\in B_{2}}{\mathbb{K}}\{b\}

in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} that become equal, X1=X2X_{1}=X_{2}, after applying the forgetful functor.

Remark 7.3.

An isomorphism φ:X→≅Y\varphi\colon X\xrightarrow{\cong}Y of evolution algebras carrying B1B_{1} to a natural basis B2=φ⁡(B1)B_{2}=\varphi(B_{1}) of YY is the prototype of the data the rigidified category NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} keeps track of. Indeed, a morphism in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} permutes the lines and rescales them, and therefore the automorphisms of an object are monomial: writing n=dimXn=\dim X,

AutNEvol𝕂nd⁡(X)≤𝕂×≀Sn,\operatorname{Aut}_{\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}}(X)\;\leq\;{\mathbb{K}}^{\times}\wr S_{n},

the group of generalized permutation (𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-monomial) matrices. Explicitly an automorphism is a pair

φ=(σ,λ1,…,λn),σ∈Sn,λi∈𝕂×,φ⁡(Ai)=λi​Aσ⁡(i).\varphi=(\sigma;\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n}),\qquad\sigma\in S_{n},\ \lambda_{i}\in{\mathbb{K}}^{\times},\qquad\varphi(A_{i})=\lambda_{i}\,A_{\sigma(i)}.

The cancellation phenomena described in Section 5 are governed by a multi-indexed refinement of an automorphism.

Every natural evolution algebra has a unique well-defined associated graph.

Definition 7.4.

Let X=⨁i=1nAiX=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}A_{i} be a natural evolution algebra over 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}. Its associated graph is the directed graph

Γ⁡(X)=(V,E),V={A1,…,An},\Gamma(X)=(V,E),\qquad V=\{A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\},

whose vertices are the one-dimensional AiA_{i}, and where (Ar,As)∈E(A_{r},A_{s})\in E if and only if the composite

Ar2↪X=⨁i=1nAi→πsAsA_{r}^{2}\;\hookrightarrow\;X=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\;\xrightarrow{\ \pi_{s}\ }\;A_{s}

is nonzero, where πs\pi_{s} is the canonical linear projection

X=⨁i=1nAi⟶πsAs,∑ixi⟼xs(xi∈Ai).\begin{array}[]{rcl}X=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}&\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\pi_{s}}}&A_{s},\\ \textstyle\sum_{i}x_{i}&\longmapsto&x_{s}\quad(x_{i}\in A_{i}).\end{array}

For a natural evolution algebra XX we set b⁡(X):=b⁡(Γ⁡(X))\operatorname{b}(X):=\operatorname{b}\bigl(\Gamma(X)\bigr).

Remark 7.5.

If A=⨁i=1nbi​𝕂A=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}{\mathbb{K}} is a non-degenerate natural evolution algebra over 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}, then B={bi}B=\{b_{i}\} is a natural base of AA and the graphs Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) and Γ⁡(A)\Gamma(A) coincide. Since the balance of non-degenerate evolution algebra is independent of the chosen natural basis (Theorem 6.1), the different notions of balance b⁡(A)\operatorname{b}(A) agree.

We now introduce a construction that will play a central role in Section 8, where it will be used to describe non-degenerate evolution algebras X,Y,ZX,Y,Z satisfying

X⊗Y≅X⊗ZX\otimes Y\cong X\otimes Z

while Y≇ZY\not\cong Z.

Definition 7.6.

Let X=⨁i=1n𝕂​biX=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}b_{i} be an object in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} with structure matrix (mk​l)(m_{kl}) associated to the basis B={bi}B=\{b_{i}\}. An mm-isomorphism of XX is an mm-tuple

Φ=(φ0,…,φm−1),φr=(σr,λr,1,…,λr,n)∈𝕂×≀Sn,\Phi=(\varphi_{0},\dots,\varphi_{m-1}),\qquad\varphi_{r}=(\sigma_{r};\lambda_{r,1},\dots,\lambda_{r,n})\in{\mathbb{K}}^{\times}\wr S_{n},

such that the scalars

μi​j:=mσr−1​(i),σr+1−1​(j)⋅λr+1,σr+1−1​(j)λr,σr−1​(i) 2\mu_{ij}\;:=\;\frac{\,m_{\,\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i)\,,\,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}\;\cdot\;\lambda_{\,r+1,\,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}\,}{\lambda_{\,r,\,\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i)}^{\,2}}

do not depend on rr (indices read modulo mm). The scalars (μi​j)(\mu_{ij}) are then the structure constants of an evolution algebra, which we denote by XΦX^{\Phi}:

XΦ:=⨁i=1n𝕂​b¯iwith structure matrix ​(μi​j).X^{\Phi}\;:=\;\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}\bar{b}_{i}\qquad\text{with structure matrix }(\mu_{ij}).

We first show that mm-isomorphisms preserve non-degeneracy for evolution algebras.

Proposition 7.7.

Let X=⨁i=1n𝕂​biX=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}b_{i} be an object in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} with structure matrix (mk​l)(m_{kl}) associated to the basis B={bi}B=\{b_{i}\}. Let Φ=(φ0,…,φm−1)\Phi=(\varphi_{0},\dots,\varphi_{m-1}) be an mm-isomorphism of XX. Then the evolution algebra XΦ=⨁i=1n𝕂​b¯iX^{\Phi}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}\bar{b}_{i} is non-degenerate, that is, it is an object in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}.

Proof.

Recall that an evolution algebra with natural basis {b1,…,bn}\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\} is non-degenerate precisely when every natural basis element has nonzero square. Equivalently, every row of its structure matrix is nonzero.

We prove that every row of the structure matrix (μi​j)(\mu_{ij}) of XΦX^{\Phi} is nonzero. Fix i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}. Choose any r∈{1,…,m}r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}. By definition,

μi​j=mσr−1​(i),σr+1−1​(j)​λr+1,σr+1−1​(j)λr,σr−1​(i)2.\mu_{ij}=\frac{m_{\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i),\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}\lambda_{r+1,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}}{\lambda_{r,\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i)}^{2}}.

Since each φr\varphi_{r} is an automorphism and φr​(bk)=λr,k​bσr​(k),\varphi_{r}(b_{k})=\lambda_{r,k}b_{\sigma_{r}(k)}, we have λr,k≠0\lambda_{r,k}\neq 0 for every rr and every kk. Hence

(9) λr+1,σr+1−1​(j)λr,σr−1​(i)2≠0\frac{\lambda_{r+1,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}}{\lambda_{r,\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i)}^{2}}\neq 0

for every i,ji,j.

Now put k=σr−1​(i).k=\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i). Since XX is non-degenerate, the kk-th row of (mi​j)(m_{ij}) is nonzero. Therefore there exists some ℓ∈{1,…,n}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,n\} such that

(10) mk​ℓ≠0.m_{k\ell}\neq 0.

Take j=σr+1​(ℓ),j=\sigma_{r+1}(\ell), or equivalently σr+1−1​(j)=ℓ.\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)=\ell. Therefore, combining Equation (9) and Equation (10),

μi​j=mσr−1​(i),σr+1−1​(j)​λr+1,σr+1−1​(j)λr,σr−1​(i)2=mk​ℓ​λr+1,ℓλr,k2≠0.\mu_{ij}=\frac{m_{\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i),\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}\lambda_{r+1,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}}{\lambda_{r,\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i)}^{2}}=\frac{m_{k\ell}\lambda_{r+1,\ell}}{\lambda_{r,k}^{2}}\neq 0.

Thus the ii-th row of (μi​j)(\mu_{ij}) is nonzero.

Since ii was arbitrary, every row of the structure matrix (μi​j)(\mu_{ij}) is nonzero. Hence every natural basis element of XΦX^{\Phi} has nonzero square. Therefore XΦX^{\Phi} is non-degenerate. ∎

Example 7.8 (The cyclic algebra CnC_{n}).

Let X=Cn=𝕂​c0⊕⋯⊕𝕂​cn−1X=C_{n}={\mathbb{K}}c_{0}\oplus\dots\oplus{\mathbb{K}}c_{n-1} be the cyclic evolution algebra with ci 2=ci+1c_{i}^{\,2}=c_{i+1} (indices mod nn), so that its structure matrix is

mi​j={1,j=i+1(modn),0,otherwise.m_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&j=i+1\pmod{n},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

For r∈ℤ/nr\in{\mathbb{Z}}/n let σr∈Sn\sigma_{r}\in S_{n} be the cyclic shift σr​(i)=i−r(modn)\sigma_{r}(i)=i-r\pmod{n} and set

φr=(σr,1,…,1)∈AutNEvol𝕂nd⁡(Cn)≤𝕂×≀Sn.\varphi_{r}=(\sigma_{r};1,\dots,1)\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}}(C_{n})\leq{\mathbb{K}}^{\times}\wr S_{n}.

Then Φ=(φ0,…,φn−1)\Phi=(\varphi_{0},\dots,\varphi_{n-1}) is an nn-isomorphism of CnC_{n}: since all scalars equal 11,

μi​j=mσr−1​(i),σr+1−1​(j)=mi+r,j+r+1={1,i=j(modn),0,otherwise,\mu_{ij}=m_{\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i),\,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}=m_{\,i+r,\;j+r+1}=\begin{cases}1,&i=j\pmod{n},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}

which is independent of rr. The corresponding algebra CnΦC_{n}^{\Phi} is therefore

CnΦ=⨁j=0n−1𝕂⁡{c¯j},c¯j 2=c¯j,C_{n}^{\Phi}=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{n-1}{\mathbb{K}}\{\bar{c}_{j}\},\qquad\bar{c}_{j}^{\,2}=\bar{c}_{j},

the split algebra 𝕂n{\mathbb{K}}^{\,n}. In particular CnΦ≇CnC_{n}^{\Phi}\not\cong C_{n} for n≥2n\geq 2.

Thus an mm-isomorphism of a non-degenerate evolution algebra XX produces a new non degenerate evolution algebra XΦX^{\Phi}, in general not isomorphic to XX.

The following result shows that two distinct mm-isomorphisms of a non-degenerate evolution algebra XX, say Φ\Phi and Φ′\Phi^{\prime}, may give rise to isomorphic evolution algebras XΦ≅XΦ′X^{\Phi}\cong X^{\Phi^{\prime}}.

Lemma 7.9.

Let X=⨁i=1n𝕂​biX=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}b_{i} be an object in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} with structure matrix (mk​l)(m_{kl}) associated to the basis B={bi}B=\{b_{i}\}. Let Φ=(φ0,…,φm−1)\Phi=(\varphi_{0},\dots,\varphi_{m-1}) be an mm-isomorphism of XX. Then every cyclic “shift” of Φ\Phi, Φ(s)=(φs,φs+1,…,φs+m−1)\Phi^{(s)}=(\varphi_{s},\varphi_{s+1},\dots,\varphi_{s+m-1}) (indices mod mm) is an mm-isomorphism of XX, and XΦ≅XΦ(s)X^{\Phi}\cong X^{\Phi^{(s)}}.

Proof.

The condition of Definition 7.6 relates only consecutive pairs φr,φr+1\varphi_{r},\varphi_{r+1}, and therefore any cyclic “shift” preserves every such pair. Moreover, by Definition 7.6 the structure constants μi​j\mu_{ij} of XΦX^{\Phi} are independent of rr; those of XΦ(s)X^{\Phi^{(s)}} are given by the same expression evaluated at r↦r+sr\mapsto r+s, hence take the identical value μi​j\mu_{ij}. Thus XΦX^{\Phi} and XΦ(s)X^{\Phi^{(s)}} carry the same structure matrix on the same basis, so XΦ=XΦ(s)X^{\Phi}=X^{\Phi^{(s)}}; in particular XΦ≅XΦ(s)X^{\Phi}\cong X^{\Phi^{(s)}}. ∎

8. Cyclic evolution algebras and cancellation I

In this section we obtain our first results on the zero divisors of 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), or equivalently, on the non-cancellation phenomena in Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} or NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}. First we need to introduce some notation.

Definition 8.1.

Let A,B,CA,B,C be evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras. We say that A⊗CA\otimes C and B⊗CB\otimes C are isomorphic relative to CC if there is an isomorphism

φ:A⊗C→≅B⊗C\varphi\colon A\otimes C\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }B\otimes C

that preserves the second tensor coordinate: for every c∈Cc\in C there is a linear map ψc:A→B\psi_{c}\colon A\to B with

φ⁡(a⊗c)=ψc​(a)⊗c(a∈A).\varphi(a\otimes c)=\psi_{c}(a)\otimes c\qquad(a\in A).

Equivalently, φ⁡(A⊗c)⊆B⊗c\varphi(A\otimes c)\subseteq B\otimes c for every c∈Cc\in C. In this case we say φ\varphi is second-coordinate preserving.

The relevance of the cyclic algebras, defined in Example 7.8, to the multiplicative structure of 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is that tensoring with CmC_{m} cancels exactly up to the mm-isomorphisms of Definition 7.6.

Theorem 8.2.

Let A,BA,B be algebras in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} of dimension nn. Then

A⊗Cm≅B⊗Cm(relative to ​Cm)A\otimes C_{m}\;\cong\;B\otimes C_{m}\qquad(\text{relative to }C_{m})

in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} if and only if there is an mm-isomorphism Φ=(φ0,…,φm−1)\Phi=(\varphi_{0},\dots,\varphi_{m-1}) of AA with B≅AΦB\cong A^{\Phi}.

Proof.

Let A=⨁i=1n𝕂​aiA=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}a_{i} and B=⨁i=1n𝕂​biB=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}b_{i}, so {ai}i=1n\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} and {bi}i=1n\{b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} are natural bases of AA and BB, with structure constants ai2=∑jmi​j​aja_{i}^{2}=\sum_{j}m_{ij}a_{j} and bi2=∑jℳi​j​bjb_{i}^{2}=\sum_{j}\mathcal{M}_{ij}b_{j}. Following the notation in Example 7.8, let Cm=⨁i=0m−1𝕂​ciC_{m}=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{m-1}{\mathbb{K}}c_{i}, so cr2=cr+1c_{r}^{2}=c_{r+1} (indices mod mm). An isomorphism

φ:A⊗Cm≅B⊗Cm(relative to ​Cm)\varphi\colon A\otimes C_{m}\;\cong\;B\otimes C_{m}\qquad(\text{relative to }C_{m})

in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} has the form

φ⁡(ai⊗cr)=φr​(ai)⊗cr=λr​i​bσr​(i)⊗cr,φr=(σr,λr​1,…,λr​n),\varphi(a_{i}\otimes c_{r})=\varphi_{r}(a_{i})\otimes c_{r}=\lambda_{ri}\,b_{\sigma_{r}(i)}\otimes c_{r},\qquad\varphi_{r}=(\sigma_{r};\lambda_{r1},\dots,\lambda_{rn}),

with one monomial map φr\varphi_{r} per layer crc_{r}. We determine when φ\varphi is an algebra isomorphism.

Orthogonality. For i≠ji\neq j,

φ⁡(ai⊗cr)​φ​(aj⊗cr)=λr​i​λr​j​(bσr​(i)​bσr​(j))⊗cr2,\varphi(a_{i}\otimes c_{r})\,\varphi(a_{j}\otimes c_{r})=\lambda_{ri}\lambda_{rj}\,(b_{\sigma_{r}(i)}b_{\sigma_{r}(j)})\otimes c_{r}^{2},

which vanishes because σr∈Sn\sigma_{r}\in S_{n} is injective, so σr​(i)≠σr​(j)\sigma_{r}(i)\neq\sigma_{r}(j) and bσr​(i)​bσr​(j)=0b_{\sigma_{r}(i)}b_{\sigma_{r}(j)}=0. This holds automatically.

Squares. On the one hand,

φ⁡((ai⊗cr)2)=φ⁡(∑jmi​j​aj⊗cr+1)=∑jmi​j​λr+1,j​bσr+1​(j)⊗cr+1,\varphi\bigl((a_{i}\otimes c_{r})^{2}\bigr)=\varphi\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{j}m_{ij}\,a_{j}\otimes c_{r+1}\Bigr)=\sum_{j}m_{ij}\,\lambda_{r+1,j}\,b_{\sigma_{r+1}(j)}\otimes c_{r+1},

while on the other,

φ​(ai⊗cr)2=(λr​i​bσr​(i)⊗cr)2=λr​i2​∑jℳσr​(i),σr+1​(j)​bσr+1​(j)⊗cr+1.\varphi(a_{i}\otimes c_{r})^{2}=(\lambda_{ri}b_{\sigma_{r}(i)}\otimes c_{r})^{2}=\lambda_{ri}^{2}\sum_{j}\mathcal{M}_{\sigma_{r}(i),\,\sigma_{r+1}(j)}\,b_{\sigma_{r+1}(j)}\otimes c_{r+1}.

Equality for all i,j,ri,j,r amounts to mi​j​λr+1,j=λr​i2​ℳσr​(i),σr+1​(j)m_{ij}\lambda_{r+1,j}=\lambda_{ri}^{2}\,\mathcal{M}_{\sigma_{r}(i),\sigma_{r+1}(j)}; substituting i=σr−1​(a)i=\sigma_{r}^{-1}(a) and j=σr+1−1​(b)j=\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(b) gives

ℳa​b=mσr−1​(a),σr+1−1​(b)​λr+1,σr+1−1​(b)λr,σr−1​(a) 2(for all ​a,b,r).\mathcal{M}_{ab}=\frac{m_{\sigma_{r}^{-1}(a),\,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(b)}\;\lambda_{r+1,\,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(b)}}{\lambda_{r,\,\sigma_{r}^{-1}(a)}^{\,2}}\qquad(\text{for all }\,a,b,r).

That the right-hand side is independent of rr is precisely the condition that Φ=(φ0,…,φm−1)\Phi=(\varphi_{0},\dots,\varphi_{m-1}) be an mm-isomorphism of AA as given in Definition 7.6, and ℳa​b=μa​b\mathcal{M}_{ab}=\mu_{ab} says exactly that B≅AΦB\cong A^{\Phi}. ∎

Example 8.3 (Non-cancellation of cyclic algebras).

In Example 7.8 it is shown that the cyclic evolution algebra CnC_{n} admits an nn-isomorphism Φ\Phi such that CnΦ=𝕂n≇CnC_{n}^{\Phi}={\mathbb{K}}^{n}\not\cong C_{n}. Therefore, according to Theorem 8.2, Cn⊗Cn≅𝕂n⊗CnC_{n}\otimes C_{n}\cong{\mathbb{K}}^{n}\otimes C_{n} while 𝕂n≇Cn{\mathbb{K}}^{n}\not\cong C_{n}, and [Cn][C_{n}] is a zero divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}).

9. Cyclic evolution algebras and cancellation II

We now generalize the results in the previous section to a more general family of cyclic evolution algebras, allowing also a “shift” of the second coordinate when making tensor with these algebras. This generalization makes sense only when the base field 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} is not algebraically closed (see Lemma 9.9 and Lemma 9.10).

Definition 9.1.

Given scalars m0,…,mn−1∈𝕂×m_{0},\dots,m_{n-1}\in{\mathbb{K}}^{\times}, the cyclic evolution algebra C⁡(m0,…,mn−1)C(m_{0},\dots,m_{n-1}) is defined as

C(m0,…,mn−1):=𝕂c0⊕⋯⊕𝕂cn−1,ci 2=mici+1(indices mod n).C(m_{0},\dots,m_{n-1}):={\mathbb{K}}c_{0}\oplus\dots\oplus{\mathbb{K}}c_{n-1},\qquad c_{i}^{\,2}=m_{i}\,c_{i+1}\quad(\text{indices mod }n).

The cyclic evolution algebra with all weights equal to 11 is Cn=C⁡(1,…,1).C_{n}=C(1,\dots,1).

Remark 9.2.

Observe that

C⁡(m0,…,mn−1)≅C⁡(1,…,1,∏i=0n−1mi2n−1−i).C(m_{0},\dots,m_{n-1})\;\cong\;C\!\left(1,\dots,1,\ \textstyle\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}m_{i}^{2^{\,n-1-i}}\right).

Indeed, if we denote by {a0,…,an−1}\{a_{0},\ldots,a_{n-1}\} the natural basis of C⁡(m0,…,mn−1)C(m_{0},\dots,m_{n-1}) and by {b0,…,bn−1}\{b_{0},\ldots,b_{n-1}\} the natural basis of C⁡(1,…,1,∏i=0n−1mi2n−1−i),C\!\left(1,\dots,1,\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}m_{i}^{2^{\,n-1-i}}\right)\!, the morphism given by ψ⁡(a0)=b0\psi(a_{0})=b_{0} and

ψ⁡(ai+1)=(∏j=0imj−2i−j)​bi+1for 0≤i≤n−2,\psi(a_{i+1})=\big(\prod_{j=0}^{i}m_{j}^{-2^{i-j}}\big)b_{i+1}\quad\text{for $0\leq i\leq n-2$,}

is the desired isomorphism. Observe that the isomorphism ψ\psi above is just a rescaling the natural bases, and therefore, it defines an isomorphism in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}. Lemma 9.9 below shows that, over an algebraically closed field, even this scalar normalizes to 11, so that C⁡(m0,…,mn−1)≅CnC(m_{0},\dots,m_{n-1})\cong C_{n} outright and, in particular, CnC_{n} is the normal form of every cyclic evolution algebra.

We do now generalize the concept of mm-isomorphism.

Definition 9.3.

Let α0,…,αm−1∈𝕂×\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1}\in{\mathbb{K}}^{\times} and k∈ℤ/mk\in{\mathbb{Z}}/m. A (k,α0,…,αm−1)(k;\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1})-isomorphism of an evolution algebra AA with structure constants (mi​j)(m_{ij}) is a sequence Φ=(φ0,…,φm−1)\Phi=(\varphi_{0},\dots,\varphi_{m-1}), φr=(σr,λr​1,…,λr​n)\varphi_{r}=(\sigma_{r};\lambda_{r1},\dots,\lambda_{rn}), such that the scalars

μi​j:=mσr−1​(i),σr+1−1​(j)​λr+1,σr+1−1​(j)λr,σr−1​(i) 2⋅αrαr+k\mu_{ij}\;:=\;\frac{m_{\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i),\,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}\;\lambda_{r+1,\,\sigma_{r+1}^{-1}(j)}}{\lambda_{r,\,\sigma_{r}^{-1}(i)}^{\,2}}\cdot\frac{\alpha_{r}}{\alpha_{r+k}}

are independent of rr (indices mod mm). As before, AΦA^{\Phi} denotes the evolution algebra on a copy of the basis of AA with structure constants (μi​j)(\mu_{ij}).

Remark 9.4.

Taking all αr\alpha_{r} equal, or more generally αr/αr+k=1\alpha_{r}/\alpha_{r+k}=1, recovers the mm-isomorphism of Definition 7.6; in particular Example 7.8 is an instance of the present notion as well.

Definition 9.5.

Let A,BA,B be evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras and let C=C⁡(α0,…,αm−1)C=C(\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1}). We say that A⊗CA\otimes C and B⊗CB\otimes C are isomorphic relative to CC shifting the second coordinate by kk if there is an isomorphism

φ:A⊗C→≅B⊗C\varphi\colon A\otimes C\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }B\otimes C

such that for every cr∈Cc_{r}\in C there is a linear map ψr:A→B\psi_{r}\colon A\to B with

φ⁡(a⊗cr)=ψr​(a)⊗cr+k(a∈A).\varphi(a\otimes c_{r})=\psi_{r}(a)\otimes c_{r+k}\qquad(a\in A).
Remark 9.6.

An isomorphism relative to C⁡(α0,…,αm−1)C(\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1}) shifting the second coordinate by 00 is just an isomorphism relative to C⁡(α0,…,αm−1)C(\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1}) as given in Definition 8.1.

Theorem 9.7.

Let A,BA,B be algebras in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} and let C=C⁡(α0,…,αm−1)C=C(\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1}). Then A⊗C≅B⊗CA\otimes C\cong B\otimes C relative to CC shifting the second coordinate by kk in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} if and only if there is a (k,α0,…,αm−1)(k;\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1})-isomorphism Φ\Phi of AA with B≅AΦB\cong A^{\Phi}.

Proof.

The computation follows that of Theorem 8.2, applied to the layer map φ⁡(ai⊗cr)=φr​(ai)⊗cr+k\varphi(a_{i}\otimes c_{r})=\varphi_{r}(a_{i})\otimes c_{r+k}. Here, the weights cr2=αr​cr+1c_{r}^{2}=\alpha_{r}c_{r+1} of CC enter the coefficient comparison, contributing an extra factor of αr/αr+k\alpha_{r}/\alpha_{r+k}. Therefore, the resulting condition is that the scalars μi​j\mu_{ij} from Definition 9.3 must be independent of rr Definition 9.3. This is equivalent to Φ\Phi being a (k,α0,…,αm−1)(k;\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1})-isomorphism with B≅AΦB\cong A^{\Phi}. ∎

Lemma 9.8.

If Φ=(φ0,…,φm−1)\Phi=(\varphi_{0},\dots,\varphi_{m-1}) is a (k,α0,…,αm−1)(k;\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1})-isomorphism of AA, then for each s∈ℤ/ms\in{\mathbb{Z}}/m the cyclic shift Φ(s)=(φs,…,φs+m−1)\Phi^{(s)}=(\varphi_{s},\dots,\varphi_{s+m-1}) is a (k,αs,…,αs+m−1)(k;\alpha_{s},\dots,\alpha_{s+m-1})-isomorphism of AA.

Proof.

As in Lemma 7.9, the defining condition constrains only consecutive indices, which a cyclic shift preserves. ∎

Over an algebraically closed field the weights of a cyclic evolution algebra can be removed altogether.

Lemma 9.9.

If 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} is algebraically closed, then C⁡(α0,…,αm−1)≅CmC(\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1})\cong C_{m} for all α0,…,αm−1∈𝕂×\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1}\in{\mathbb{K}}^{\times}.

Proof.

Seek an isomorphism c¯i↦γi​ci\bar{c}_{i}\mapsto\gamma_{i}c_{i} from C⁡(α0,…,αm−1)C(\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1}) (with c¯i2=αi​c¯i+1\bar{c}_{i}^{2}=\alpha_{i}\bar{c}_{i+1}) to CmC_{m} (with ci2=ci+1c_{i}^{2}=c_{i+1}). Comparing φ⁡(c¯i2)=αi​γi+1​ci+1\varphi(\bar{c}_{i}^{2})=\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i+1}c_{i+1} with φ​(c¯i)2=γi2​ci+1\varphi(\bar{c}_{i})^{2}=\gamma_{i}^{2}c_{i+1} forces the recursion γi+1=γi2/αi\gamma_{i+1}=\gamma_{i}^{2}/\alpha_{i}, whence

γi=γ0 2i​∏j=0i−1αj−2i−1−j.\gamma_{i}=\gamma_{0}^{\,2^{i}}\prod_{j=0}^{i-1}\alpha_{j}^{-2^{\,i-1-j}}.

Closing the cycle (γm=γ0\gamma_{m}=\gamma_{0}, indices mod mm) gives γ0 2m−1=∏j=0m−1αj 2m−1−j\gamma_{0}^{\,2^{m}-1}=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\alpha_{j}^{\,2^{\,m-1-j}}, so it suffices to take

γ0=(∏j=0m−1αj 2m−1−j)1/(2m−1)∈𝕂×,\gamma_{0}=\Bigl(\textstyle\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\alpha_{j}^{\,2^{\,m-1-j}}\Bigr)^{1/(2^{m}-1)}\in{\mathbb{K}}^{\times},

which exists because 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} is algebraically closed. The remaining γi\gamma_{i} are then nonzero, so φ\varphi is an isomorphism. ∎

Lemma 9.10.

Let A,BA,B be evolution 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras and let C=C⁡(α0,…,αm−1)C=C(\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m-1}). If 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} is algebraically closed, then A⊗C≅B⊗CA\otimes C\cong B\otimes C relative to CC shifting the second coordinate by kk if and only if A⊗Cm≅B⊗CmA\otimes C_{m}\cong B\otimes C_{m} relative to CmC_{m}.

Proof.

Write C=⨁i=0m−1𝕂​c¯iC=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{m-1}{\mathbb{K}}\bar{c}_{i} and Cm=⨁i=0m−1𝕂​ciC_{m}=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{m-1}{\mathbb{K}}c_{i}. Then, by Lemma 9.9, there exists an isomorphism in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}

ψ:C→Cmc¯i↦γi​ci\begin{array}[]{rcl}\psi\colon C&\to&C_{m}\\ \bar{c}_{i}&\mapsto&\gamma_{i}c_{i}\end{array}

Moreover, for any given l∈ℤl\in{\mathbb{Z}}, there exists an automorphism in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}

Ψl:Cm→Cmci↦ci+l(indices mod m)\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Psi_{l}\colon C_{m}&\to&C_{m}\\ c_{i}&\mapsto&c_{i+l}\quad\text{(indices mod $m$)}\end{array}

Therefore, ϕ:A⊗C→B⊗C\phi\colon A\otimes C\to B\otimes C is an isomorphism relative to CC shifting the second coordinate by kk if and only if ϕ~:A⊗Cm→B⊗Cm,\widetilde{\phi}\colon A\otimes C_{m}\to B\otimes C_{m}, given by

ϕ~=(IdB⊗(Ψ−k∘ψ))∘ϕ∘(IdA⊗ψ−1)\widetilde{\phi}=\big(\mathrm{Id}_{B}\otimes(\Psi_{-k}\circ\psi)\big)\circ\phi\circ(\mathrm{Id}_{A}\otimes\psi^{-1})

is an isomorphism relative to CmC_{m}. ∎

10. Local monomorphisms, transfer of isomorphism, and balance

In this section we show that the isomorphism type of tensor products in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} is indeed controlled by local data of the common factor, and that non-cancellation phenomena appears when this common factor has higher balance.

We first define how we do compare the local data of two evolution algebras.

Definition 10.1.

Let A=⨁i∈I𝕂​aiA=\bigoplus_{i\in I}{\mathbb{K}}a_{i} and B=⨁p∈P𝕂​bpB=\bigoplus_{p\in P}{\mathbb{K}}b_{p} be objects in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} with associated structure matrices (mi​j)(m_{ij}) and (ℳp​q)(\mathcal{M}_{pq}) respectively, and let φ:A→B\varphi\colon A\to B be a linear map of the form φ⁡(ai)=bσ⁡(i)\varphi(a_{i})=b_{\sigma(i)} for some index map σ:I→P.\sigma\colon I\to P. We call φ\varphi a local monomorphism if

mi​j≠0impliesℳσ⁡(i)​σ​(j)≠0(for all​i,j).m_{ij}\neq 0\quad\text{implies}\quad\mathcal{M}_{\sigma(i)\sigma(j)}\neq 0\qquad(\text{for all}\ i,j).
Remark 10.2.

A local monomorphism A→BA\to B is exactly a morphism of graphs Γ⁡(A)→Γ⁡(B)\Gamma(A)\to\Gamma(B): the identity of Definition 10.1 says precisely that each edge ai→aja_{i}\to a_{j} of Γ⁡(A)\Gamma(A) is matched by an edge bσ⁡(i)→bσ⁡(j)b_{\sigma(i)}\to b_{\sigma(j)} of Γ⁡(B)\Gamma(B). The governing invariant of such graphs is the balance of Definition 2.2 and Definition 2.4; it coincides with the invariant of Elduque–Labra [8, 9] and, on the graph side, with that of Lovász [10, p. 154].

We show that the isomorphism type of tensor products in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} is transferred by local monomorphisms.

Theorem 10.3.

Suppose A⊗C≅B⊗CA\otimes C\cong B\otimes C relative to CC in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}, and suppose there is a local monomorphism Ψ:D→C\Psi\colon D\to C. Then A⊗D≅B⊗DA\otimes D\cong B\otimes D relative to DD in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}.

Proof.

Write

A=⨁i=1n𝕂ai,B=⨁i=1n𝕂bi,C=⨁i=1m𝕂ci,andD=⨁i=1l𝕂di,A=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}a_{i},\quad B=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}b_{i},\quad C=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}{\mathbb{K}}c_{i},\quad\text{and}\quad D=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{l}{\mathbb{K}}d_{i},

and let (mi​j)(m_{ij}), (ℳi​j)(\mathcal{M}_{ij}), and (γi​j)(\gamma_{ij}) the associated structure matrices of AA, BB and CC.

Let φ⁡(ai⊗cr)=λr,i​bσr​(i)⊗cr\varphi(a_{i}\otimes c_{r})=\lambda_{r,i}\,b_{\sigma_{r}(i)}\otimes c_{r} be the given isomorphism relative to CC. Then

φ⁡((ai⊗cr)2)=∑j,smi​j​γr​s​λs,j​bσs​(j)⊗cs,\varphi\bigl((a_{i}\otimes c_{r})^{2}\bigr)=\sum_{j,s}m_{ij}\,\gamma_{rs}\,\lambda_{s,j}\,b_{\sigma_{s}(j)}\otimes c_{s},

while

φ​(ai⊗cr)2=∑j,sλr,i2​γr​s​ℳσr​(i),σs​(j)​bσs​(j)⊗cs,\varphi(a_{i}\otimes c_{r})^{2}=\sum_{j,s}\lambda_{r,i}^{2}\,\gamma_{rs}\,\mathcal{M}_{\sigma_{r}(i),\,\sigma_{s}(j)}\,b_{\sigma_{s}(j)}\otimes c_{s},

so the two agree provided that

(11) mi​j​λs,j=λr,i2​ℳσr​(i),σs​(j)whenever γr​s≠0.m_{ij}\,\lambda_{s,j}=\lambda_{r,i}^{2}\,\mathcal{M}_{\sigma_{r}(i),\,\sigma_{s}(j)}\quad\text{whenever $\gamma_{rs}\neq 0$}.

Let Ψ⁡(d)=cρ⁡(d)\Psi(d)=c_{\rho(d)} be the local monomorphism, with index map ρ\rho. Define

φ¯:A⊗D⟶B⊗Dai⊗d⟼λρ⁡(d),i​bσρ⁡(d)​(i)⊗d\begin{array}[]{rcl}\bar{\varphi}\colon A\otimes D&\longrightarrow&B\otimes D\\ a_{i}\otimes d&\longmapsto&\lambda_{\rho(d),\,i}\,b_{\sigma_{\rho(d)}(i)}\otimes d\end{array}

which is relative to DD. Orthogonality is automatic: products of elements with distinct second coordinates vanish on both sides, and for a fixed dd the map σρ⁡(d)\sigma_{\rho(d)} is injective, so ai​aj=0a_{i}a_{j}=0 (i≠ji\neq j) is preserved. For the squares, write d2=∑d′Md​d′​d′d^{2}=\sum_{d^{\prime}}M_{dd^{\prime}}d^{\prime}. Then

while

We can now connect the balance invariant to the zero-divisors in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}). Recall that [A][A] is a zero-divisor if [A]​([Y]−[Z])=0[A]\bigl([Y]-[Z]\bigr)=0 for some Y≇ZY\not\cong Z, i.e. if A⊗Y≅A⊗ZA\otimes Y\cong A\otimes Z with Y≇ZY\not\cong Z. The canonical example of a zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is [Cn][C_{n}] (Example 8.3).

Theorem 10.4.

Let DD be an indecomposable object in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} with b⁡(D)>1\operatorname{b}(D)>1, and let nn be a divisor of b⁡(D)\operatorname{b}(D). If A⊗Cn≅B⊗CnA\otimes C_{n}\cong B\otimes C_{n} relative to CnC_{n}, then A⊗D≅B⊗DA\otimes D\cong B\otimes D relative to DD.

Write D=⨁i=1m𝕂​diD=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}{\mathbb{K}}d_{i}. Since DD is indecomposable and non-degenerate, the graph Γ⁡(D)\Gamma(D) is connected and has no sinks. Thus, according to Lemma 2.8, there exists a map

hn:{di:i=1,…,m}⟶ℤ/n,h_{n}\colon\{d_{i}:i=1,\ldots,m\}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}/n,

such that if (di,dj)(d_{i},d_{j}) is an edge in Γ⁡(D)\Gamma(D) then hn​(dj)=hn​(di)+1(modn).h_{n}(d_{j})=h_{n}(d_{i})+1\pmod{n}. Setting

11. Cancellation when the balance is one

The results above show that high balance forces zero-divisors. We now prove the complementary statement: a balance-one indecomposable factor cancels. The proof relies on a non-trivial translation of Lovász’s combinatorial arguments [10, pp. 153–155] into the setting of evolution algebras, requiring several modifications to handle the algebraic structure.

Theorem 11.1.

Let CC be an indecomposable object in NEvol𝕂nd\nevol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} with b⁡(C)=1\operatorname{b}(C)=1. If A⊗C≅B⊗CA\otimes C\cong B\otimes C relative to CC, then A≅BA\cong B.

Proof.

Let

A=⨁i=1n𝕂ai,B=⨁i=1n𝕂bi,andC=⨁i=1m𝕂ciA=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}a_{i},\quad B=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{K}}b_{i},\quad\text{and}\quad C=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}{\mathbb{K}}c_{i}

and let (γi​j)(\gamma_{ij}) be the associated structure matrix of CC.

Given φ:A⊗C≅B⊗C\varphi\colon A\otimes C\cong B\otimes C relative to CC, write φ⁡(ai⊗cr)=φr​(ai)⊗cr\varphi(a_{i}\otimes c_{r})=\varphi_{r}(a_{i})\otimes c_{r}, where

φr:A⟶Bai⟼λi,r​bσr​(i)\begin{array}[]{rcl}\varphi_{r}\colon A&\longrightarrow&B\\ a_{i}&\longmapsto&\lambda_{i,r}\,b_{\sigma_{r}(i)}\end{array}

is a monomial linear isomorphism. Notice that each φr\varphi_{r} sends lines to lines, thus it preserves orthogonality, and it is an algebra isomorphism as soon as it respects squares.

Now, the identity φ⁡((ai⊗cr)2)=φ​(ai⊗cr)2\varphi((a_{i}\otimes c_{r})^{2})=\varphi(a_{i}\otimes c_{r})^{2} expands to

∑sγr,s​φs​(ai2)⊗cs=∑sγr,s​φr​(ai)2⊗cs,\sum_{s}\gamma_{r,s}\,\varphi_{s}(a_{i}^{2})\otimes c_{s}=\sum_{s}\gamma_{r,s}\,\varphi_{r}(a_{i})^{2}\otimes c_{s},

so that

(13) (cr,cr′)∈Γ⁡(C)⟹φr​(ai)2=φr′​(ai2)(for all​i).(c_{r},c_{r^{\prime}})\in\Gamma(C)\ \Longrightarrow\ \varphi_{r}(a_{i})^{2}=\varphi_{r^{\prime}}(a_{i}^{2})\quad(\text{for all}\ i).

Writing j=σr​(i)j=\sigma_{r}(i), and taking into account that φr\varphi_{r} and φr′\varphi_{r^{\prime}} are linear isomorphism, Equation (13) reads

(14) (cr,cr′)∈Γ⁡(C)⟹φr−1​(bj)2=φr′−1​(bj2)(for all​j).(c_{r},c_{r^{\prime}})\in\Gamma(C)\ \Longrightarrow\ \varphi_{r}^{-1}(b_{j})^{2}=\varphi_{r^{\prime}}^{-1}(b_{j}^{2})\quad(\text{for all}\ j).

Step 1 (composition along edges). For any sequence of edges (cr1,cr1′),…,(cr2​k+1,cr2​k+1′)(c_{r_{1}},c_{r_{1}^{\prime}}),\dots,(c_{r_{2k+1}},c_{r_{2k+1}^{\prime}}) in Γ⁡(C)\Gamma(C), applying Equation (13) and Equation (14) alternately yields:

(15) (φr2​k+1φr2​k−1⋯φr1)(a)2=(φr2​k+1′φr2​k′−1⋯φr1′)(a2).\bigl(\varphi_{r_{2k+1}}\varphi_{r_{2k}}^{-1}\cdots\varphi_{r_{1}}\bigr)(a)^{2}=\bigl(\varphi_{r_{2k+1}^{\prime}}\varphi_{r_{2k}^{\prime}}^{-1}\cdots\varphi_{r_{1}^{\prime}}\bigr)(a^{2}).
