Remark 11.2.

Theorem 11.1is the converse, for indecomposable factors, of Theorem A under mild hypothesis: an indecomposable CC with b⁡(C)=1\operatorname{b}(C)=1 cancels relative to CmC_{m}, whereas b⁡(C)>1\operatorname{b}(C)>1 makes it a zero-divisor.

12. Indecomposability of Tensor Products

As noted in Section 5, understanding the ring generators of 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) requires identifying when the tensor product of two indecomposable algebras remains indecomposable. We first show that the balance of the factors provides lower bounds for the number of summands in the optimal direct-sum decomposition into indecomposable evolution ideals [3, Theorem 5.11].

Theorem 12.1.

Let X1,X2∈Evol𝕂ndX_{1},X_{2}\in\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} be indecomposable, di=b⁡(Xi)d_{i}=\operatorname{b}(X_{i}), and d=gcd⁡(d1,d2)d=\gcd(d_{1},d_{2}). Then

X1⊗X2=⨁c=0d−1IcX_{1}\otimes X_{2}=\bigoplus_{c=0}^{d-1}I_{c}

where each IcI_{c} is a non-trivial evolution ideal of X1⊗X2X_{1}\otimes X_{2}.

Proof.

Let BiB_{i} be a natural basis of XiX_{i}, with associated structure matrix (wr​s(i))(w^{(i)}_{rs}), for i=1,2i=1,2. First, recall that

Γ⁡(X1⊗X2,B1⊗B2)=Γ⁡(X1,B1)×Γ⁡(X2,B2).\Gamma(X_{1}\otimes X_{2},B_{1}\otimes B_{2})=\Gamma(X_{1},B_{1})\times\Gamma(X_{2},B_{2}).

Set ni=dim(Xi)n_{i}=\dim(X_{i}). Since d=gcd⁡(d1,d2)d=\gcd(d_{1},d_{2}), Lemma 2.8 yields surjective maps

hi:{1,…,ni}→ℤ/dh_{i}\colon\{1,\ldots,n_{i}\}\to{\mathbb{Z}}/d

such that, whenever (r,s)∈Γ⁡(Xi,Bi)(r,s)\in\Gamma(X_{i},B_{i}) one has

hi​(s)=hi​(r)+1.h_{i}(s)=h_{i}(r)+1.

Define H⁡(r,s)=h1​(r)−h2​(s)∈ℤ/d.H(r,s)=h_{1}(r)-h_{2}(s)\in{\mathbb{Z}}/d. Every edge ((r,s),(k,l))\big((r,s),(k,l)\big) in Γ⁡(X1⊗X2,B1⊗B2)\Gamma(X_{1}\otimes X_{2},B_{1}\otimes B_{2}) then satisfies

H⁡(k,l)=(h1​(r)+1)−(h2​(s)+1)=H⁡(r,s),H(k,l)=\bigl(h_{1}(r)+1\bigr)-\bigl(h_{2}(s)+1\bigr)=H(r,s),

so HH is constant on each connected component of the graph. For c∈ℤ/dc\in{\mathbb{Z}}/d set

Ic=span𝕂⁡{b1,r⊗b2,s∈B1⊗B2:H⁡(r,s)=c}.I_{c}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{K}}\{\,b_{1,r}\otimes b_{2,s}\in B_{1}\otimes B_{2}:H(r,s)=c\,\}.

For a basis vector in IcI_{c}, (b1,r⊗b2,s)2=∑k,lwr​k(1)​ws​l(2)​(b1,k⊗b2,l)(b_{1,r}\otimes b_{2,s})^{2}=\sum_{k,l}w^{(1)}_{rk}w^{(2)}_{sl}\,(b_{1,k}\otimes b_{2,l}), and every contributing (k,l)(k,l) has H⁡(k,l)=cH(k,l)=c, so the square lies in IcI_{c}. Moreover products of distinct natural basis vectors vanish, so each IcI_{c} is an evolution ideal. Since B1⊗B2B_{1}\otimes B_{2} is partitioned by the values of HH,

X1⊗X2=⨁c∈ℤ/dIc,X_{1}\otimes X_{2}=\bigoplus_{c\in{\mathbb{Z}}/d}I_{c},

and surjectivity of maps h​(i)dh(i)_{d} makes all IcI_{c} non-empty. ∎

Example 12.2.

We can follow along the lines in the proof of Theorem 12.1 to completely describe the tensor product of cyclic evolution algebras (compare [10, Eq. (5)]):

Cn⊗Cm≅Clcm⁡(n,m)⊗𝕂gcd⁡(n,m).C_{n}\otimes C_{m}\cong C_{\lcm(n,m)}\otimes{\mathbb{K}}^{\gcd(n,m)}.

Equivalently, Cn⊗CmC_{n}\otimes C_{m} is a direct sum of gcd⁡(n,m)\gcd(n,m) copies of Clcm⁡(n,m)C_{\lcm(n,m)}.

Indeed, b⁡(Cn)=n\operatorname{b}(C_{n})=n, b⁡(Cm)=m\operatorname{b}(C_{m})=m, and if d=gcd⁡(n,m)d=\gcd(n,m), then the maps hi,dh_{i,d} are just the mod⁡d\operatorname{mod}d reduction and therefore, for any c∈ℤ/dc\in{\mathbb{Z}}/d one has:

Ic\displaystyle I_{c} =span𝕂{ck​d+c⊗cs:k=0,…,nd−1;s=0,…,m−1;c=smodd}\displaystyle=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{K}}\{c_{kd+c}\otimes c_{s}:k=0,\ldots,\frac{n}{d}-1;\,s=0,\ldots,m-1;\,c=s\mod{d}\}
≅Cnd​m=Clcm⁡(n,m).\displaystyle\cong C_{\frac{n}{d}m}=C_{\lcm(n,m)}.

Therefore

Cn⊗Cm=⨁c∈ℤ/dIc≅⨁c∈ℤ/dClcm⁡(n,m)≅Clcm⁡(n,m)⊗𝕂gcd⁡(n,m).C_{n}\otimes C_{m}=\bigoplus_{c\in{\mathbb{Z}}/d}I_{c}\cong\bigoplus_{c\in{\mathbb{Z}}/d}C_{\lcm(n,m)}\cong C_{\lcm(n,m)}\otimes{\mathbb{K}}^{\gcd(n,m)}.

Notice that Theorem 12.1 identifies a necessary condition for the tensor product to be indecomposable.

Corollary 12.3.

Let X1,X2∈Evol𝕂ndX_{1},X_{2}\in\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} be indecomposable, di=b⁡(Xi)d_{i}=\operatorname{b}(X_{i}), and d=gcd⁡(d1,d2)d=\gcd(d_{1},d_{2}). If X1⊗X2X_{1}\otimes X_{2} is indecomposable, then d=1d=1.

The converse of Corollary 12.3 holds, and we can now give a complete characterization of indecomposable tensor products. The following is a reinterpretation of [5, Theorem 15] in evolution-algebra form.

Theorem 12.4.

Let X1,X2∈Evol𝕂ndX_{1},X_{2}\in\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} be indecomposable, and di=b⁡(Xi)d_{i}=\operatorname{b}(X_{i}). Then X1⊗X2X_{1}\otimes X_{2} is indecomposable if and only if gcd⁡(d1,d2)=1\gcd(d_{1},d_{2})=1, and in that case b⁡(X1⊗X2)=d1​d2\operatorname{b}(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})=d_{1}d_{2}.

Proof.

Recall that the algebra XiX_{i} is non-degenerate. Hence, the graph Γ⁡(Xi,Bi)\Gamma(X_{i},B_{i}) has no sinks and has non-trivial balance for any natural basis BiB_{i} of XiX_{i}. Moreover, the notion of balance used here agrees with the notion of weight in [5] (see Remark 2.5). Since, for non-degenerate evolution algebras, indecomposability is equivalent to weak connectedness of the associated graph [3], the statement follows directly from [5, Theorem 15]. ∎

There is also a multiplicative description of indecomposability for iterated tensor products, the evolution-algebra form of [5, Corollary 16], which we record here.

Proposition 12.5.

Let X1,…,Xk∈Evol𝕂ndX_{1},\dots,X_{k}\in\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} be indecomposable. Then X1⊗⋯⊗XkX_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X_{k} is indecomposable if and only if the balances b⁡(X1),…,b⁡(Xk)b(X_{1}),\dots,b(X_{k}) are pairwise coprime, and in that case

b(X1⊗⋯⊗Xk)=∏i=1kb(Xi).b\bigl(X_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X_{k}\bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}b(X_{i}).

13. Zero-divisors among direct sums of cyclic algebras

Conjecture 1.1predicts that an algebra of Evol𝕂nd\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}} is a zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) precisely when every one of its indecomposable direct summands has balance strictly greater than 11. The sufficiency direction holds in full generality: Theorem A produces a zero-divisor relation for any direct sum ⨁jXj\bigoplus_{j}X_{j} all of whose summands have balance >1>1, by combining the relations of the summands through Lemma 5.3. The necessity direction is known only for indecomposable algebras (Remark 11.2, via the cancellation Theorem 11.1), and its extension to reducible algebras is a natural open problem. In this section we settle it for arbitrary direct sums of cyclic algebras.

We now introduce the main object of study of this section.

Definition 13.1.

Let ℛ⊆𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) be the subring generated by the classes of the cyclic algebras {[Cn]:n≥1}\{[C_{n}]:n\geq 1\}, where C1=𝕂C_{1}={\mathbb{K}} is the unit.

By Example 12.2 the product of two generators is a single generator up to an integer factor,

(21) [Cn]​[Cm]=gcd⁡(n,m)​[Clcm⁡(n,m)],[C1]=1,[C_{n}]\,[C_{m}]=\gcd(n,m)\,[C_{\lcm(n,m)}],\qquad[C_{1}]=1,

so products of generators never leave the ℤ\mathbb{Z}-span of {[Cn]}\{[C_{n}]\}. As the CnC_{n} are pairwise non-isomorphic indecomposables, their classes are part of the free ℤ\mathbb{Z}-basis of 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}); hence

ℛ=⨁n≥1ℤ⁡[Cn]\mathcal{R}=\bigoplus_{n\geq 1}\mathbb{Z}\,[C_{n}]

is free abelian on {[Cn]}\{[C_{n}]\}, with multiplication given by Equation (21).

For a positive integer FF, write τ⁡(F)\tau(F) for its number of divisors, and define

ℛF=⨁d|Fℤ⁡[Cd]⊆ℛ.\mathcal{R}_{F}=\bigoplus_{d\mid F}\mathbb{Z}\,[C_{d}]\subseteq\mathcal{R}.

Since d|Fd\mid F and e|Fe\mid F imply that lcm⁡(d,e)|F\lcm(d,e)\mid F, each ℛF\mathcal{R}_{F} is a subring of ℛ\mathcal{R}, free of rank τ⁡(F)\tau(F), and ℛ=⋃FℛF\mathcal{R}=\bigcup_{F}\mathcal{R}_{F}.

We now construct balance characters for ℛ\mathcal{R}.

Lemma 13.2.

For each integer m≥1m\geq 1 there is a unique ring homomorphism χm:ℛ→ℤ\chi_{m}\colon\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{Z} with

χm​([Cn])={n,n|m,0,n∤m.\chi_{m}\bigl([C_{n}]\bigr)=\begin{cases}n,&n\mid m,\\[2.0pt] 0,&n\nmid m.\end{cases}
Proof.

Define χm\chi_{m} on the basis by the formula given in the statement, and extend it ℤ\mathbb{Z}-linearly. Uniqueness is then immediate. It remains to verify that χm\chi_{m} is a ring homomorphism.

Unitality is χm​([C1])=1\chi_{m}([C_{1}])=1. For multiplicativity it suffices to check the generators. Using Equation (21), we obtain

χm​([Cn]​[Cn′])={gcd⁡(n,n′)​lcm⁡(n,n′),if lcm⁡(n,n′)|m,0,otherwise.\chi_{m}\bigl([C_{n}][C_{n^{\prime}}]\bigr)=\begin{cases}\gcd(n,n^{\prime})\,\lcm(n,n^{\prime}),&\text{if $\lcm(n,n^{\prime})\mid m$,}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

while

χm​([Cn])​χm​([Cn′])={n​n′,if n|m and n′|m,0,otherwise.\chi_{m}\bigl([C_{n}]\bigr)\chi_{m}\bigl([C_{n^{\prime}}]\bigr)=\begin{cases}nn^{\prime},&\text{if $n\mid m$ and $n^{\prime}\mid m$,}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

These agree because gcd⁡(n,n′)​lcm⁡(n,n′)=n​n′\gcd(n,n^{\prime})\lcm(n,n^{\prime})=nn^{\prime}, and lcm⁡(n,n′)|m\lcm(n,n^{\prime})\mid m if and only if n|mn\mid m and n′|mn^{\prime}\mid m. ∎

The character χm\chi_{m} records the total dimension contributed by the cyclic summands whose balance divides mm. In particular, χ1​([X])\chi_{1}([X]) counts the copies of the unit algebra 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} occurring as summands of XX. These characters diagonalize the cyclic subring after tensoring with ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Proposition 13.3.

For every F≥1F\geq 1, the map

ΦF:ℛF⊗ℚ⟶∏m|Fℚ,ξ⟼(χm​(ξ))m|F\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Phi_{F}\colon\mathcal{R}_{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q}&\longrightarrow&\prod_{m\mid F}\mathbb{Q},\\ \xi&\longmapsto&\bigl(\chi_{m}(\xi)\bigr)_{m\mid F}\end{array}

is an isomorphism of ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebras. Consequently ℛF⊗ℚ≅ℚτ⁡(F)\mathcal{R}_{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q}\cong\mathbb{Q}^{\tau(F)} is a product of fields, and ℛ⊗ℚ\mathcal{R}\otimes\mathbb{Q} is reduced.

Proof.

Each coordinate of ΦF\Phi_{F} is a ring homomorphism, so ΦF\Phi_{F} is a homomorphism between two ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebras of the same dimension τ⁡(F)\tau(F). It therefore suffices to show ΦF\Phi_{F} is injective, that is, that the matrix of ΦF\Phi_{F} in the basis {[Cd]:d∣F}\{[C_{d}]:d\mid F\} of the source and the coordinate basis of the target, namely

M=(χm​([Cd]))m|F,d|FM=\bigl(\chi_{m}([C_{d}])\bigr)_{m\mid F,\;d\mid F}

is invertible. List the divisors of FF in standard increasing numerical order. A nonzero entry

Mm,d=χm​([Cd])=dM_{m,d}=\chi_{m}([C_{d}])=d

requires d|md\mid m, hence d≤md\leq m, and therefore MM is lower triangular while its diagonal entries are Mm,m=mM_{m,m}=m. Thus

detM=∏d|Fd=Fτ⁡(F)2≠0,\det M=\prod_{d\mid F}d=F^{\frac{\tau(F)}{2}}\neq 0,

and ΦF\Phi_{F} is an isomorphism. Passing to the union over FF, every element of ℛ⊗ℚ\mathcal{R}\otimes\mathbb{Q} lies in some ℛF⊗ℚ\mathcal{R}_{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q}, which is reduced; hence ℛ⊗ℚ\mathcal{R}\otimes\mathbb{Q} is reduced. ∎

Now we can characterize the zero-divisors in ℛ\mathcal{R}.

Corollary 13.4.

An element α=∑nan​[Cn]∈ℛ\alpha=\sum_{n}a_{n}[C_{n}]\in\mathcal{R} is a zero-divisor in ℛ\mathcal{R} if and only if there exists m≥1m\geq 1 such that

χm​(α)=∑n|man​n=0.\chi_{m}(\alpha)=\sum_{n\mid m}a_{n}\,n=0.
Proof.

Choose FF with α∈ℛF\alpha\in\mathcal{R}_{F}. As ℛ\mathcal{R} is free abelian, hence torsion-free, α\alpha is a zero-divisor in ℛ\mathcal{R} if and only if it is one in ℛ⊗ℚ\mathcal{R}\otimes\mathbb{Q}, and a witness may be taken in some ℛF′⊗ℚ\mathcal{R}_{F^{\prime}}\otimes\mathbb{Q} with F|F′F\mid F^{\prime}. Under the isomorphism ΦF′\Phi_{F^{\prime}} of Proposition 13.3, zero-divisors of the product ∏m|F′ℚ\prod_{m\mid F^{\prime}}\mathbb{Q} are exactly the tuples with a vanishing coordinate, so α\alpha is a zero-divisor if and only if χm​(α)=0\chi_{m}(\alpha)=0 for some m|F′m\mid F^{\prime}. Finally, for any mm one has χm|ℛF=χgcd⁡(m,F)\chi_{m}|_{\mathcal{R}_{F}}=\chi_{\gcd(m,F)} because n|Fn\mid F forces n|m⇔n|gcd⁡(m,F)n\mid m\Leftrightarrow n\mid\gcd(m,F); thus the existence of a vanishing coordinate is independent of the truncation, and is equivalent to χm​(α)=0\chi_{m}(\alpha)=0 for some m≥1m\geq 1. ∎

Corollary 13.4characterizes the zero-divisors of ℛ\mathcal{R} (inside ℛ\mathcal{R}). The next lemma extends this characterization to the entire Grothendieck ring: a relation that does not occur within ℛ\mathcal{R} cannot arise after allowing the test element to range over arbitrary elements of 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}). The argument relies on the fact that elements of ℛ\mathcal{R} are integral over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, together with the torsion-freeness of 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}).

Lemma 13.5.

Let α∈ℛ\alpha\in\mathcal{R}.

  1. (1)

    If χm​(α)≠0\chi_{m}(\alpha)\neq 0 for every m≥1m\geq 1, then α\alpha is a non-zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}).

  2. (2)

    If χm​(α)=0\chi_{m}(\alpha)=0 for some m≥1m\geq 1, then α\alpha is a zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), with a witness already in ℛ\mathcal{R}.

Proof.

Fix FF with α∈ℛF\alpha\in\mathcal{R}_{F}.

(1): If no character vanishes on α\alpha, then ΦF​(α)\Phi_{F}(\alpha) has all coordinates nonzero, so α\alpha is a unit in ℛF⊗ℚ≅ℚτ⁡(F)\mathcal{R}_{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q}\cong\mathbb{Q}^{\tau(F)}. Let β∈ℛF⊗ℚ\beta\in\mathcal{R}_{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q} be its inverse and clear denominators: there exist an integer c≥1c\geq 1 and an element δ=c​β∈ℛF\delta=c\beta\in\mathcal{R}_{F} with

α​δ=cinℛF⊆𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd).\alpha\,\delta=c\quad\text{in}\quad\mathcal{R}_{F}\subseteq\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}).

Now suppose α​W=0\alpha W=0 for some W∈𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)W\in\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}). Then

c​W=(α​δ)​W=δ⁡(α​W)=0,cW=(\alpha\delta)W=\delta(\alpha W)=0,

and since 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is free abelian, hence torsion-free, and c≠0c\neq 0, we get W=0W=0. Thus α\alpha is a non-zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}).

(2): If χm0​(α)=0\chi_{m_{0}}(\alpha)=0, then ΦF​(α)\Phi_{F}(\alpha) has a vanishing coordinate, so α\alpha is a zero-divisor in ℛF⊗ℚ\mathcal{R}_{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q}. Clearing denominators in an identity α​η0=0\alpha\eta_{0}=0 with 0≠η0∈ℛF⊗ℚ0\neq\eta_{0}\in\mathcal{R}_{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q} yields 0≠η∈ℛF0\neq\eta\in\mathcal{R}_{F} with α​η=0\alpha\eta=0 in ℛF⊆𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{R}_{F}\subseteq\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}). As η≠0\eta\neq 0 in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), α\alpha is a zero-divisor there. ∎

The key point in the proof of Lemma 13.5.(1) is that the test element WW may be an arbitrary element of 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}): it need not be cyclic, nor even a direct sum of indecomposable elements of bounded balance. Nevertheless, the relation

α​δ=c⋅1,\alpha\delta=c\cdot 1,

which holds in ℛ\mathcal{R}, implies that c​W=0cW=0. This is illustrated in the following example.

Example 13.6.

Let α=[𝕂⊕C2]=1+[C2]\alpha=[{\mathbb{K}}\oplus C_{2}]=1+[C_{2}]. Then, taking δ=3​[𝕂]−[C2]=3−[C2],\delta=3[{\mathbb{K}}]-[C_{2}]=3-[C_{2}], one has

(1+[C2])​(3−[C2])=3,\bigl(1+[C_{2}]\bigr)\bigl(3-[C_{2}]\bigr)=3,

since [C2]2=[C2⊗C2]=[C2⊕C2]=2​[C2][C_{2}]^{2}=[C_{2}\otimes C_{2}]=[C_{2}\oplus C_{2}]=2[C_{2}]. So any WW satisfying (1+[C2])​W=0(1+[C_{2}])W=0 also satisfies 3​W=03W=0 and hence W=0W=0. Therefore, [𝕂⊕C2][{\mathbb{K}}\oplus C_{2}] is not a zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), even though its summand C2C_{2} itself is a zero-divisor.

Finally, we can describe the non-degenerate algebras whose optimal direct-sum decomposition into indecomposable evolution ideals involve just cyclic algebras, and give rise to zero-divisors in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}).

Theorem 13.7.

Let X=⨁i=1rCniX=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}C_{n_{i}} be a finite direct sum of cyclic algebras, with ni≥1n_{i}\geq 1. Then [X][X] is a zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) if and only if ni>1n_{i}>1 for every ii; equivalently, if and only if every indecomposable direct summand of XX has balance greater than 11. In particular, Conjecture 1.1 holds for all direct sums of cyclic algebras.

Proof.

The indecomposable summands of XX are the cyclic algebras CniC_{n_{i}}, which have balance b⁡(Cni)=nib(C_{n_{i}})=n_{i}; so the two formulations of the condition coincide. Write α=[X]=∑i[Cni]∈ℛ\alpha=[X]=\sum_{i}[C_{n_{i}}]\in\mathcal{R}, so that for every m≥1m\geq 1

χm(α)=∑{i:ni∣m}ni≥0,\chi_{m}(\alpha)=\sum_{\{i\,:\,n_{i}\mid m\}}n_{i}\;\geq 0,

a sum of positive integers, which vanishes exactly when no nin_{i} divides mm.

If some ni0=1n_{i_{0}}=1, then ni0|mn_{i_{0}}\mid m for every mm, so χm​(α)≥1>0\chi_{m}(\alpha)\geq 1>0 for all mm. Therefore, by Lemma 13.5.(1), α\alpha is a non-zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}).

If instead ni>1n_{i}>1 for all ii, then no nin_{i} divides m=1m=1, so χ1​(α)=0\chi_{1}(\alpha)=0; by Lemma 13.5.(2), α\alpha is a zero-divisor in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}), with a witness in ℛ\mathcal{R}. ∎

Remark 13.8.

Observe that Theorem 13.7 clarifies the statement of Remark 1.2. Indeed, Theorem 13.7 handles the necessity direction when all summands are cyclic, without invoking the reduction given by Lemma 5.3. Instead, it works directly in 𝒢⁡(Evol𝕂nd)\mathcal{G}(\evol^{\mathrm{nd}}_{\mathbb{K}}) via the balance characters of ℛ\mathcal{R} introduced in Lemma 13.2.
